topics.name: The nature of the economic problem

questions.q: What is the basic economic problem?
questions.why: Scarcity forces choices about what to produce, how and for whom.

questions.q: Which of the following is a free good?
questions.why: Sea water exists in such quantity that no resources are needed to provide it, so it has no opportunity cost; the others all use scarce resources.

questions.q: Why is a television an economic good?
o: Scarce resources are used to make it, so it has an opportunity cost
It is bought mainly by consumers
questions.why: An economic good uses up scarce resources that could have made something else, so producing it has an opportunity cost.

questions.q: A city council has a budget of $5 billion but receives requests for projects costing $8 billion. Which economic concept does this illustrate?
questions.why: The council has finite resources and more wants than it can meet, so it faces scarcity and must choose.

questions.q: Which statement about human wants is correct in economics?
o: Wants are the same as needs
Wants are fully satisfied in developed countries
Wants are unlimited: people always want more goods and services
questions.why: Wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are finite; this is why scarcity exists in every economy.

long.q: Explain the difference between an economic good and a free good, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: an economic good is scarce: making it uses resources, so it has an opportunity cost
B1: example, e.g. a car / a loaf of bread
B1: a free good is not scarce: it needs no resources to make, so there is no opportunity cost
B1: example, e.g. air / sea water / sunlight

long.q: Define scarcity.
scheme: B1: a situation where there are not enough (finite) resources
B1: to satisfy everyone's unlimited wants

long.q:
Extract: Lakeland city council has a budget of $40 million this year. Residents have asked for a new hospital wing ($25 million), a bridge ($20 million) and a park ($6 million).
Using the extract, identify two pieces of evidence that Lakeland council faces the basic economic problem.
scheme: B1: the requests total $51 million but the budget is only $40 million (wants exceed resources)
B1: the council cannot fund all three projects, so it must choose between them

long.q: Analyse how the basic economic problem affects both consumers and producers.
scheme: B1: consumers have limited incomes but unlimited wants
B1: so they must choose which goods and services to buy, giving up others
B1: e.g. a family that buys a new car may not be able to afford a holiday
B1: producers have limited resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise)
B1: so they must decide what to produce and how, e.g. a farmer using a field for wheat cannot use it for maize
B1: in both cases every choice has an opportunity cost because resources are scarce

long.q:
Extract: Over the last 20 years real GDP in Northland has doubled. Average incomes are much higher, yet a recent survey found that most households still want better housing, newer technology and more holidays.
Discuss whether economic growth will ever solve the basic economic problem in Northland.
scheme: B1: growth means more goods and services can be produced, so more wants can be met
B1: application: Northland's output has doubled, so living standards and choice have increased
B1: growth may also lift people out of poverty and meet basic needs such as food and shelter
B1: however, wants are unlimited: as incomes rise people want more and better products
B1: application: the survey shows households still want better housing, technology and holidays
B1: resources remain finite, e.g. land and some raw materials cannot grow without limit, and growth may use them up
B1: so scarcity remains and choices with opportunity costs still have to be made
B1: justified conclusion: growth can reduce the severity of the problem for some needs, but it cannot solve it, because wants grow faster than finite resources

questions.q: A farmer uses a tractor to plough a field. Which factor of production is the tractor?
questions.why: Capital is a man-made good used to produce other goods and services.

questions.q: Which is an example of land as a factor of production?
questions.why: Land covers all natural resources, including fish stocks; buildings and vans are capital and the programmer is labour.

questions.q: What is the reward for enterprise?
questions.why: Entrepreneurs organise the other factors and take risks, and are rewarded with profit.

questions.q: A coal miner retrains as a solar-panel fitter. This shows an increase in the…
questions.why: Occupational mobility is the ease of moving between jobs; retraining gives the worker new skills for a different occupation.

questions.q: Which is most likely to increase the quality of a country's labour force?
o: A fall in the birth rate
A rise in the retirement age
questions.why: Training raises workers' skills and productivity; the retirement age changes the quantity of labour, not its quality.

long.q: Identify the four factors of production and state the reward to each.
scheme: B1: land: rent
B1: labour: wages
B1: capital: interest
B1: enterprise: profit

long.q: Define enterprise as a factor of production.
scheme: B1: the willingness and ability to organise the other factors of production
B1: and to take the risks of running a business (in the hope of profit)

long.q: Explain two reasons why labour may be geographically immobile.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. housing costs are much higher in the area where jobs are available
B1: explained, e.g. workers cannot afford to move even if they find a job there
B1: a second reason, e.g. family and social ties / children's schooling / lack of information about vacancies / cost of moving
B1: explained, e.g. workers are unwilling to leave relatives and friends, so they stay in areas of high unemployment

long.q:
Extract: Mineland's government has spent $2 billion on new ports and fast broadband. Net immigration of 200 000 working-age people a year is increasing the labour force, and a new national apprenticeship scheme has started.
Analyse how these changes in the quantity and quality of factors of production could increase Mineland's productive capacity.
scheme: B1: the ports and broadband increase the quantity of capital
B1: capital makes workers and firms more productive, e.g. goods can be shipped faster and services supplied online
B1: immigration increases the quantity of labour available
B1: so firms can employ more workers and produce more output
B1: apprenticeships raise the quality of labour (skills), increasing output per worker
B1: with more and better factors the economy's maximum possible output rises (the PPC shifts outwards)

long.q: Discuss whether a government should spend more on education and training rather than on capital such as roads to increase the quality of its factors of production.
scheme: B1: education and training raise the skills and productivity of labour
B1: this improves occupational mobility and reduces structural unemployment
B1: skilled workers can use new technology, attracting firms and investment
B1: however, the benefits of education take many years to appear
B1: roads and other capital reduce transport costs for all firms quickly
B1: without good infrastructure, even skilled workers cannot produce efficiently
B1: the opportunity cost of each depends on what the country lacks most
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. both are complementary; spend more on training where skills shortages are the main constraint and on roads where poor infrastructure limits output

questions.q: Opportunity cost is…
o: the money price of a good
the next best alternative given up
questions.why: Choosing one option means losing the benefit of the next best.

questions.q: Sara spends $20 on a book. Her next choice would have been a cinema ticket, and her third choice a meal. What is the opportunity cost of the book?
questions.why: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative given up, which is the cinema ticket.

questions.q: A firm uses its factory to make bicycles instead of scooters, which was its next best option. What is the opportunity cost of making the bicycles?
o: The cost of the steel used
The scooters it could have made instead
questions.why: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which here is the scooters the factory could have produced.

questions.q: Opportunity cost exists because…
o: resources are scarce and have alternative uses
money is used to buy goods
questions.why: Using scarce resources for one thing means they cannot be used for another, so every choice gives something up.

questions.q: Mina is offered two jobs: Job X pays $500 a week and Job Y pays $450 a week. She takes Job X. What is the opportunity cost of taking Job X?
o: Job Y and its $450 a week
Nothing, because Job X pays more
questions.why: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative, Job Y, even though Job X pays more.

long.q: Define opportunity cost and explain, using an example, the opportunity cost a government faces when it decides to spend more on healthcare.
scheme: B1: opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
B1: the government's resources (tax revenue) are scarce, so spending more on healthcare means less can be spent elsewhere
B1: example: the next best use given up, e.g. new schools or roads that cannot now be built

long.q:
Extract: Ravi earns $15 an hour working as a plumber for customers. Last Saturday he spent 6 hours repairing the roof of his own house instead of working.
Calculate the opportunity cost, in money terms, of Ravi repairing his own roof.
scheme: A1: $90 of income given up

long.q: Explain the opportunity cost to a young person of choosing to go to university rather than getting a job.
scheme: B1: opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up
B1: the young person gives up the wages they could have earned while studying
B1: they also give up work experience and the chance of earlier promotion
B1: the choice is worthwhile if the future benefits, e.g. higher graduate pay, are greater than this cost

long.q:
Extract: Delta Motors has $50 million to invest this year. It can either build a new electric-car factory or upgrade its existing petrol-car production lines. It decides to build the electric-car factory.
Analyse the opportunity cost of Delta Motors' decision.
scheme: B1: the firm's funds are limited (scarce), so it cannot do both projects
B1: the opportunity cost is the upgrade of the petrol-car lines that is given up
B1: so the petrol-car lines may stay less efficient, with higher average costs
B1: Delta may lose sales and profit on petrol cars in the short term
B1: but the electric-car factory may bring greater future revenue as demand for electric cars grows
B1: the decision is sensible if the expected benefit of the factory is greater than the benefit given up

long.q:
Extract: The government of Westria plans to spend $4 billion on a high-speed railway between its two largest cities. Critics say the money could instead build 40 new hospitals.
Discuss whether the Westria government should spend $4 billion on the railway, considering the opportunity cost.
scheme: B1: the opportunity cost of the railway is the next best alternative, e.g. the 40 hospitals
B1: the railway cuts journey times, so firms and workers become more productive
B1: it may create jobs in construction and attract investment, raising economic growth and tax revenue
B1: hospitals improve health, so fewer working days are lost and quality of life rises
B1: without new hospitals, waiting times may grow and the poor may suffer most
B1: the railway may run over budget, and its benefits go mainly to people in two cities
B1: the decision depends on which gives the greater benefit to society and on the country's most urgent needs
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. if health care is already overstretched the hospitals should come first; if transport is the main constraint on growth the railway is justified

questions.q: A shift outwards of a production possibility curve shows…
questions.why: More or better resources let the economy produce more of both goods.

questions.q: A point inside a country's production possibility curve shows that…
o: the economy is using all its resources efficiently
the output is unattainable with current resources
some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
questions.why: Inside the curve the economy could produce more of both goods, so some resources are idle or wasted.

questions.q: A point outside a country's production possibility curve is…
o: unattainable with current resources and technology
a combination with no opportunity cost
questions.why: The PPC shows the maximum possible output; points beyond it cannot be reached unless resources or technology improve.

questions.q: A PPC shows cars on one axis and wheat on the other. New technology raises productivity in car production only. What happens to the PPC?
o: The whole curve shifts outwards equally
The economy moves along the curve towards more cars
The curve pivots outwards on the car axis; the maximum wheat output is unchanged
questions.why: Only the maximum output of cars rises, so the curve swings outwards along the car axis while the wheat intercept stays the same.

questions.q: An economy moves along its PPC from 50 computers and 200 tonnes of rice to 60 computers and 170 tonnes of rice. What is the opportunity cost of each extra computer?
questions.why: 30 tonnes of rice are given up for 10 more computers, so each computer costs 30 ÷ 10 = 3 tonnes of rice.

long.q: An economy can produce these combinations of food and machines: A 100 food and 0 machines; B 90 food and 10 machines; C 70 food and 20 machines; D 40 food and 30 machines. Calculate the opportunity cost of increasing the output of machines from 10 to 20, and from 20 to 30, and explain why it changes.
scheme: B1: from 10 to 20 machines: 20 units of food given up (2 food per machine)
B1: from 20 to 30 machines: 30 units of food given up (3 food per machine)
B1: the opportunity cost rises as more machines are made
B1: because resources are not equally suited to both goods: the resources moved later are better at making food than machines

long.q: Explain two causes of an outward shift of a country's production possibility curve.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. an increase in the quantity of resources (more workers through immigration, more capital through investment)
B1: explained: the economy can produce more of both goods, so the maximum output rises
B1: a second cause, e.g. an improvement in the quality of resources (education and training, better technology)
B1: explained: each resource becomes more productive

long.q: Define a production possibility curve.
scheme: B1: a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods (or services) that an economy can produce
B1: when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed

long.q:
Extract: In Southland, 8% of the labour force was unemployed. Then an earthquake destroyed 15% of the country's factories and roads.
Analyse, using a production possibility curve diagram described in words, the effects of these events on Southland's economy.
scheme: B1: unemployment means production is at a point inside the PPC
B1: the economy produces less than it could, so output is lost
B1: the earthquake reduces the quantity of capital
B1: so the PPC shifts inwards towards the origin
B1: the maximum possible output of both goods falls
B1: rebuilding and reducing unemployment could move production back to the curve and, over time, shift the PPC outwards again

long.q: Discuss whether a country should move resources from producing consumer goods to producing capital goods.
scheme: B1: on a PPC with consumer goods and capital goods, this is a movement along the curve towards capital goods
B1: the opportunity cost is the consumer goods given up, so living standards fall now
B1: more capital goods (machines, infrastructure) increase productive capacity
B1: so the PPC shifts outwards in future, allowing more of both goods
B1: however, in a poor country cutting consumption may leave people without basic needs
B1: the capital goods may be poorly chosen or take many years to raise output
B1: the right balance depends on current living standards and how productive the new capital will be
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. a gradual shift towards capital goods is worthwhile where basic needs are already met, because future growth outweighs the short-term sacrifice

questions.q: Which is a microeconomic issue?
o: The price of coffee in a city market
questions.why: Microeconomics studies individual markets and decision makers, such as one market for coffee.

questions.q: Which is a macroeconomic issue?
o: A firm deciding how many workers to hire
A household choosing between two holidays
A fall in the country's real GDP
questions.why: Real GDP measures the output of the whole economy, so it is a macroeconomic issue.

questions.q: Macroeconomics is the study of…
o: the costs of a single firm
questions.why: Macroeconomics looks at aggregates such as total output, inflation and unemployment.

questions.q: A government raises the tax on cigarettes to reduce smoking. Which decision maker is acting, and at which level of the economy?
questions.why: The government is intervening in one particular market (cigarettes), which is a microeconomic decision.

questions.q: Which pair are both studied in microeconomics?
o: Price elasticity of demand and wage rates in an industry
The government budget and the current account
questions.why: PED and an industry's wage rates concern individual markets; the other pairs are whole-economy issues.

long.q: Define macroeconomics.
scheme: B1: the study of the economy as a whole
B1: e.g. total output, inflation, unemployment and economic growth

long.q:
Extract: A news bulletin reports: (1) Sunrise Bakery has cut the price of its bread by 10%; (2) national unemployment has risen to 7%; (3) workers at one hotel chain have won a 4% pay rise; (4) inflation has fallen to 2%.
Identify one microeconomic item and one macroeconomic item from the bulletin.
scheme: B1: microeconomic: Sunrise Bakery's price cut / the hotel workers' pay rise
B1: macroeconomic: national unemployment of 7% / inflation of 2%

long.q: Explain the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics, using one example of each.
scheme: B1: microeconomics studies individual decision makers and markets (households, firms, single industries)
B1: example, e.g. how the price of rice is set / a firm's costs
B1: macroeconomics studies the whole economy
B1: example, e.g. the national inflation rate / economic growth / unemployment

long.q: Analyse how a macroeconomic decision by the government, such as raising interest rates, can affect microeconomic decision makers.
scheme: B1: higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for households
B1: so households cut spending on items bought on credit, such as cars and houses
B1: saving becomes more rewarding, so households save more and spend less
B1: firms face higher costs of borrowing to invest
B1: so they may cancel investment and, with lower sales, employ fewer workers
B1: so a decision about the whole economy changes prices, output and employment in individual markets

long.q: Discuss whether a large rise in the world price of oil is only a microeconomic issue.
scheme: B1: it is a microeconomic issue because it changes price and quantity in one market, the oil market
B1: oil firms earn more revenue and may supply more; consumers buy less petrol
B1: it also affects related markets, e.g. demand for electric cars rises
B1: however, oil is used by almost all firms, so costs of production rise across the economy
B1: this can cause cost-push inflation, a macroeconomic issue
B1: higher costs may cut output and employment, reducing economic growth
B1: for an oil-importing country the current account may worsen
B1: justified conclusion: it starts as a microeconomic change but, because oil is so widely used, it has major macroeconomic effects, so it is not only microeconomic

topics.name: The role of markets in allocating resources

questions.q: Which are the three basic economic questions every economy must answer?
o: What to produce, how to produce it and for whom
How much to tax, how much to spend and how much to borrow
When to export, when to import and when to save
Who works, who retires and who studies
questions.why: Because resources are scarce, every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.q: In a market economy, what mainly decides which goods are produced?
o: The price mechanism, through consumer demand and profit
questions.why: Firms produce what consumers are willing to pay for, because that is where profits are made.

questions.q: A market is in disequilibrium when…
o: quantity demanded does not equal quantity supplied at the current price
questions.why: Disequilibrium means there is excess demand or excess supply at the current price.

questions.q: Demand for electric bikes rises sharply. Through the price mechanism, what is most likely to happen next?
o: Price falls and resources leave the industry
Price stays the same and the shortage continues
The government decides to make more bikes
Price rises, profits rise and more resources move into making electric bikes
questions.why: A higher price signals consumer demand and gives firms an incentive to move resources into that market.

questions.q: In a market economy, the "for whom" question is answered mainly by…
questions.why: Goods go to those willing and able to pay the market price, so income determines who receives them.

long.q: Define the price mechanism.
scheme: B1: the system in which prices are set by the interaction of demand and supply (buyers and sellers) in markets
B1: and those prices allocate resources, signalling what to produce

long.q:
Extract: In Coastia, demand for avocados has risen sharply as they became fashionable. The price rose from $2.00 to $3.50 per kg in a year. Many farmers switched land and workers from growing maize to growing avocados.
Identify the signalling function and the incentive function of price in the extract.
scheme: B1: signalling: the higher price ($2.00 to $3.50) signals that consumers want more avocados
B1: incentive: the higher price and profit encourage farmers to switch land and workers to avocados

long.q: Explain how the price mechanism answers the "how to produce" question.
scheme: B1: firms aim to make the most profit, so they want the lowest-cost method of production
B1: they choose the combination of factors according to the relative prices of those factors
B1: e.g. if wages are high compared with the cost of machines, firms use capital-intensive methods
B1: so the least-cost method uses fewer of the scarcest (most expensive) resources

long.q:
Extract: In Coastia, demand for avocados has risen sharply as they became fashionable. The price rose from $2.00 to $3.50 per kg in a year. Many farmers switched land and workers from growing maize to growing avocados.
Analyse how the price mechanism reallocated resources between maize and avocados in Coastia.
scheme: B1: the rise in demand created excess demand for avocados at the old price of $2.00
B1: so the price rose to $3.50, rationing avocados to those most willing and able to pay
B1: the higher price made avocado farming more profitable
B1: so farmers moved land and labour from maize to avocados (the supply of avocados extended)
B1: the supply of maize fell, so the price of maize may rise
B1: resources moved to the product consumers value most, without any government decision

long.q: Discuss whether the price mechanism is the best way to decide "for whom" goods and services are produced.
scheme: B1: in a market, goods go to those willing and able to pay the price
B1: this rewards hard work and enterprise, as higher earners can buy more
B1: it is quick and needs no costly government planning
B1: prices ration goods efficiently towards those who value them most
B1: however, people with low incomes may be unable to afford essentials such as health care
B1: ability to pay is not the same as need, so inequality can increase
B1: governments can correct this, e.g. by providing some services free or giving benefits
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. the price mechanism works well for most goods, but for essentials such as health and education a mix of markets and government provision is better

questions.q: If the price of a good rises, what happens to the quantity demanded?
questions.why: A movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

questions.q: Which causes the demand curve for tea to shift right?
o: A fall in the price of tea
A rise in the price of coffee (a substitute)
A rise in the price of tea
questions.why: A dearer substitute makes people switch to tea at every price.

questions.q: Market demand is…
o: the demand of the richest consumer
the quantity supplied by all firms
the demand when the price is zero
the sum of all individual consumers' demand at each price
questions.why: Market demand adds up what every buyer in the market would buy at each price.

questions.q: Bread and butter are complements. If the price of bread rises, the demand curve for butter will…
o: show a movement downwards along the curve
questions.why: Less bread is bought, so people want less butter to go with it at every price.

questions.q: At a price of $4, consumer A demands 3 units, consumer B 5 units and consumer C 2 units. They are the only buyers. What is market demand at $4?
questions.why: Market demand is the sum of individual demand: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 units.

long.q: Define demand.
scheme: B1: the willingness and ability to buy a product
B1: at a given price in a given time period

long.q:
Extract: The weekly demand schedule for orange juice in a town is: at $1, 800 cartons; at $2, 600 cartons; at $3, 400 cartons.
Using the schedule, calculate the change in quantity demanded when the price rises from $1 to $3, and state whether this is shown by a movement along or a shift of the demand curve.
scheme: B1: a fall of 400 cartons (800 − 400)
B1: a movement along the demand curve (a contraction in demand)
long.ans: Fall of 400 cartons; a movement along the curve

long.q: Explain two factors, other than price, that could cause the demand for smartphones to increase.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. a rise in incomes
B1: explained: consumers can afford more at each price, so the demand curve shifts to the right
B1: a second factor, e.g. successful advertising / a fall in the price of mobile data (a complement) / changes in tastes / a larger population
B1: explained with its effect on demand at every price

long.q:
Extract: In Riverland, the number of people aged over 65 rose by 20% in ten years. Last year the government cut the price of bus and train tickets by 30%.
Analyse how these changes may affect the demand for taxi journeys in Riverland.
scheme: B1: buses and trains are substitutes for taxis
B1: the 30% fall in their price makes them more attractive, so some people switch away from taxis
B1: so the demand curve for taxi journeys shifts to the left
B1: older people may be less able to drive or walk long distances
B1: so a larger elderly population could increase demand for taxis, shifting the curve to the right
B1: the overall effect depends on which change is stronger

long.q: Discuss whether advertising is the most important factor influencing the demand for a product such as soft drinks.
scheme: B1: advertising aims to change tastes and preferences, increasing demand at each price
B1: soft drinks are a crowded market with many brands, so advertising can win customers from rivals
B1: it builds brand loyalty, so demand stays high
B1: however, other factors also shift demand, e.g. incomes
B1: prices of substitutes such as bottled water or juices also matter
B1: health concerns or a sugar tax may reduce demand whatever the advertising
B1: weather and seasons strongly affect demand for cold drinks
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. advertising matters most between competing brands, but total demand for soft drinks depends more on incomes, health trends and prices

questions.q: Supply is the…
o: willingness and ability of producers to sell a product at a given price in a given time period
amount of a product that consumers want to buy
amount of a product held in stock
questions.why: Supply looks at the producers' side of the market at each possible price.

questions.q: Which would shift the supply curve of rice to the left?
o: A rise in the price of rice
Floods destroying part of the crop
questions.why: Floods reduce the amount that can be supplied at every price; a change in the price of rice itself causes a movement along the curve.

questions.q: Why does a supply curve usually slope upwards from left to right?
o: Consumers buy more at higher prices
Higher prices make production more profitable, so firms supply more
Costs of production fall as price rises
The government requires firms to supply more
questions.why: A higher price covers higher costs and raises potential profit, so producers offer more for sale.

questions.q: An indirect tax of $2 per unit is placed on producers of sugar. What happens to the supply curve?
o: It shifts to the right by $2
It shifts to the left, upwards by $2 at each quantity
questions.why: The tax adds $2 to the cost of supplying each unit, so supply decreases.

questions.q: Three firms are the only suppliers in a market. At $10 they supply 40, 25 and 35 units. What is market supply at $10?
questions.why: Market supply is the sum of all firms' supply: 40 + 25 + 35 = 100 units.

long.q: Explain two factors that could cause the supply of a product to increase.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. lower costs of production (raw materials, wages)
B1: explained: more profitable to produce at each price, so the supply curve shifts right
B1: a second factor, e.g. improved technology / a subsidy / good weather
B1: explained with its effect on supply

long.q: Define market supply.
scheme: B1: the total supply of a product by all producers in the market
B1: at each price (the sum of individual firms' supply)

long.q:
Extract: The monthly supply schedule for pens from a factory is: at $0.50, 2000 pens; at $1.00, 3500 pens; at $1.50, 4500 pens.
Calculate the extension in supply when the price rises from $0.50 to $1.50, and state why producers supply more at a higher price.
scheme: B1: a higher price makes production more profitable / covers the higher costs of extra output

long.q:
Extract: Cocoa farmers in Westia face mixed news. A drought has cut this year's harvest. The government has introduced a subsidy of $50 per tonne, and new disease-resistant cocoa trees are now being planted.
Analyse how these events would affect the supply of cocoa from Westia.
scheme: B1: the drought reduces the quantity that can be produced at every price
B1: so the supply curve shifts to the left
B1: the subsidy lowers producers' costs per tonne
B1: so it is more profitable to supply at each price and the supply curve shifts to the right
B1: disease-resistant trees raise yields and reduce losses, shifting supply to the right in the longer term
B1: the overall effect depends on the size of each change; in the short run the drought may dominate

long.q: Discuss whether the supply of fresh fruit is more affected by changes in the weather than the supply of manufactured goods such as phones.
scheme: B1: fruit growing depends on natural conditions such as rainfall and temperature
B1: so droughts, floods or frost can cut fruit supply sharply and unexpectedly
B1: fruit takes months to grow, so farmers cannot quickly replace a lost crop
B1: phones are made in factories, so weather has little direct effect on supply
B1: phone supply is more affected by costs of components, technology and wages
B1: however, extreme weather can still disrupt factories and transport, e.g. floods closing plants
B1: greenhouses and irrigation reduce the effect of weather on some fruit
B1: justified conclusion: fruit supply is generally more weather-dependent, though the gap depends on farming methods and how far phone supply chains are exposed to weather events

questions.q: Equilibrium price is the price at which…
o: price equals the cost of production
questions.why: At equilibrium the market clears, with no excess demand or excess supply.

questions.q: A market has this schedule: at $2, 90 demanded and 30 supplied; at $3, 70 demanded and 50 supplied; at $4, 60 demanded and 60 supplied; at $5, 50 demanded and 75 supplied. What is the equilibrium price?
questions.why: At $4 quantity demanded (60) equals quantity supplied (60).

questions.q: At a price of $6, quantity demanded is 200 and quantity supplied is 350. There is…
questions.why: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 350 − 200 = 150, so there is a surplus.

questions.q: When there is excess demand in a free market, the price will tend to…
questions.why: Buyers compete for scarce goods, so sellers can raise the price until demand and supply are equal.

questions.q: On a demand and supply diagram, the market equilibrium is shown…
o: where the demand curve meets the vertical axis
where the demand and supply curves intersect
at the highest point of the supply curve
where the two curves are furthest apart
questions.why: The intersection gives the price and quantity at which demand equals supply.

long.q: Explain what happens in a free market when the price is above the equilibrium price.
scheme: B1: at that price quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
B1: so there is excess supply (a surplus) and unsold goods build up
B1: sellers cut their price to sell their stock
B1: quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls until equilibrium is reached

long.q: Define equilibrium price.
scheme: B1: the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
B1: so the market clears and there is no pressure for the price to change

long.q:
Extract: The demand and supply schedule for tickets to a stadium concert is: at $40, 9000 demanded and 3000 supplied; at $60, 7000 demanded and 5000 supplied; at $80, 6000 demanded and 6000 supplied; at $100, 4000 demanded and 7000 supplied.
Identify the equilibrium price and calculate the excess demand at a price of $60.
scheme: B1: equilibrium price = $80
B1: excess demand at $60 = 7000 − 5000 = 2000 tickets

long.q:
Extract: The demand and supply schedule for tickets to a stadium concert is: at $40, 9000 demanded and 3000 supplied; at $60, 7000 demanded and 5000 supplied; at $80, 6000 demanded and 6000 supplied; at $100, 4000 demanded and 7000 supplied.
Analyse what would happen if the organiser set the ticket price at $40.
scheme: B1: at $40 quantity demanded is 9000 but quantity supplied is only 3000
B1: so there is excess demand (a shortage) of 6000 tickets
B1: many fans cannot get tickets and long queues or online waiting lists form
B1: a resale (black) market may develop, with tickets sold above $40
B1: in a free market, the organiser would raise the price
B1: as the price rises, demand contracts and supply extends until equilibrium at $80 and 6000 tickets

long.q: Discuss whether markets always move quickly to their equilibrium price.
scheme: B1: when there is a surplus, sellers cut prices to clear unsold stock
B1: when there is a shortage, sellers can raise prices as buyers compete
B1: in markets such as shares or foreign currency, prices change within seconds
B1: however, some prices are fixed for long periods, e.g. printed menus or catalogues
B1: wages are often set by contracts, so the labour market adjusts slowly
B1: supply may take time to respond, e.g. new houses take years to build
B1: government controls such as maximum prices can stop prices reaching equilibrium
B1: justified conclusion: markets with flexible prices and good information move quickly, but many markets adjust slowly or are prevented from reaching equilibrium

questions.q: Frost destroys part of the coffee harvest. Demand is unchanged. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of coffee?
questions.why: Supply shifts to the left, creating a shortage at the old price, so price rises and the quantity traded falls.

questions.q: Demand for umbrellas increases during a wet season while supply is unchanged. What happens?
questions.why: Demand shifts to the right, so price rises and supply extends, increasing the quantity traded.

questions.q: Supply of a product increases and demand for it decreases at the same time. Which must happen?
questions.why: Both shifts push the price down; the effect on quantity depends on which shift is larger.

questions.q: New technology lowers the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the market for solar panels?
o: Demand shifts to the right and price rises
Supply shifts to the right, price falls and quantity rises
Supply shifts to the left and price rises
Demand shifts to the left and price falls
questions.why: Lower costs increase supply at every price, so the equilibrium price falls and more panels are sold.

questions.q: The price of coach travel, a substitute for train travel, falls. What happens in the market for train journeys?
o: Demand falls, so equilibrium price and quantity fall
questions.why: Travellers switch to cheaper coaches, so demand for train journeys shifts left, lowering both price and quantity.

long.q: State two causes of a fall in the equilibrium price of a product.
scheme: B1: a decrease in demand, e.g. a change in tastes / a fall in the price of a substitute
B1: an increase in supply, e.g. lower costs of production / improved technology

long.q:
Extract: Before the harvest, mangoes sold at $2.00 per kg, with 5000 kg sold per day. After a bumper harvest, the price fell to $1.60 per kg and sales rose to 6000 kg per day.
Calculate the percentage change in the price of mangoes and the change in total daily spending on mangoes.
scheme: B1: spending falls from $10 000 to $9600, a fall of $400

long.q: Explain, using a demand and supply diagram described in words, the effect of a rise in incomes on the market for restaurant meals.
scheme: B1: higher incomes shift the demand curve for restaurant meals to the right
B1: at the original price there is now excess demand
B1: so the equilibrium price rises
B1: and supply extends, so the equilibrium quantity of meals rises

long.q:
Extract: Oil-exporting countries have agreed to cut their output by 2 million barrels a day. At the same time, demand for oil from fast-growing economies is rising.
Analyse the effect of these changes on the equilibrium price and quantity of oil.
scheme: B1: the output cut shifts the supply curve of oil to the left
B1: on its own this raises price and reduces quantity
B1: rising demand shifts the demand curve to the right
B1: on its own this raises both price and quantity
B1: both changes push the price up, so the equilibrium price rises
B1: the effect on quantity is uncertain: it rises if the demand increase is larger than the supply decrease, and falls if it is smaller

long.q:
Extract: The population of Capital City is growing by 3% a year and house prices rose by 12% last year. The government plans to release land to build 50 000 new homes over five years.
Discuss whether building more homes will reduce house prices in Capital City.
scheme: B1: new homes increase supply, shifting the supply curve of housing to the right
B1: with demand unchanged, this would lower the equilibrium price
B1: 50 000 homes is a significant addition, so it may slow price rises
B1: however, demand is also rising as the population grows by 3% a year
B1: if demand rises faster than supply, prices will still rise
B1: the homes take five years to build, so supply responds slowly
B1: other factors, e.g. low interest rates or rising incomes, may keep demand growing
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. building more homes will probably slow the rise in prices rather than reduce them, unless supply grows faster than demand

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand is −0.5. Demand is…
questions.why: Its value is less than 1 (ignoring the sign), so quantity changes less than price.

questions.q: The price of bus tickets rises by 10% and the quantity demanded falls by 4%. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.why: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = −4 ÷ 10 = −0.4.

questions.q: Demand for a product is price elastic. If the firm cuts its price, its total revenue will…
questions.why: With elastic demand the percentage rise in quantity sold is greater than the percentage fall in price, so revenue rises.

questions.q: Which product is likely to have the most price-elastic demand?
o: One brand of chocolate bar among many
questions.why: A single brand has many close substitutes, so buyers switch easily when its price rises.

questions.q: The price of a good rises from $10 to $12 and the quantity demanded falls from 500 to 450 units. What happens to total revenue?
questions.why: Revenue rises from $10 × 500 = $5000 to $12 × 450 = $5400, an increase of $400, because demand is inelastic (PED = −0.5).

long.q: The price of a good falls from $5 to $4 and the quantity demanded rises from 100 to 130 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity = +30%, % change in price = −20%
B1: elastic (greater than 1, ignoring the sign)

long.q: Define price elasticity of demand.
scheme: B1: a measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded
B1: to a change in the product's own price (% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price)

long.q: Explain two factors that make the demand for a product price inelastic.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. few close substitutes
B1: explained: when price rises, consumers have little to switch to, so quantity demanded falls only a little
B1: a second factor, e.g. the product is a necessity / takes a small share of income / is habit-forming / the time period is short
B1: explained, e.g. a box of matches takes so little of income that a price rise is hardly noticed

long.q:
Extract: City Transit raised the metro fare from $2.00 to $2.50. Daily journeys fell from 400 000 to 380 000. Some commuters said they would buy bicycles or cars if fares stayed high.
Analyse whether the fare rise was a good decision for City Transit's revenue.
scheme: A1: PED = −5 ÷ 25 = −0.2, so demand is price inelastic
B1: revenue before = $2.00 × 400 000 = $800 000 a day
B1: revenue after = $2.50 × 380 000 = $950 000 a day, a rise of $150 000
B1: revenue rose because the percentage fall in journeys was smaller than the percentage rise in fare
B1: but demand may become more elastic over time as commuters buy bicycles or cars, so revenue gains may shrink
long.ans: PED = −0.2; revenue rises by $150 000 a day

long.q: Discuss whether a government should tax products with price-inelastic demand, such as cigarettes, to raise revenue.
scheme: B1: when demand is inelastic, a tax raises price but quantity demanded falls only a little
B1: so the government collects a large and reliable tax revenue
B1: the revenue can fund public services, e.g. health care for smoking-related illness
B1: a higher price may still cut consumption a little, reducing harm and external costs
B1: however, because demand is inelastic the tax does little to reduce smoking
B1: such taxes are regressive: poorer smokers spend a larger share of their income on them
B1: very high taxes may encourage smuggling and illegal sales, reducing revenue
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. taxing inelastic products is effective for raising revenue, but if the aim is to cut consumption it should be combined with bans on advertising and health education

questions.q: Price elasticity of supply for a product is 2.0. This means that…
o: a 1% rise in price causes a 2% rise in quantity supplied
a 2% rise in price causes a 1% rise in quantity supplied
questions.why: PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price, so a value of 2 means quantity changes twice as much as price.

questions.q: The price of a product rises by 20% and the quantity supplied rises by 5%. What is the PES?
questions.why: PES = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so supply is price inelastic. PES is positive because price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

questions.q: Which factor makes supply more price elastic?
o: Firms hold large stocks of finished goods
The product takes a long time to grow
Factors of production are highly specialised and cannot be moved
questions.why: Firms with large stocks can increase the quantity supplied quickly when price rises.

questions.q: Why is the supply of fresh flowers usually price inelastic in the short run?
o: It takes months to grow more, so output cannot respond quickly to price
questions.why: Supply elasticity depends on how quickly output can change; growing time limits the response.

questions.q: A vertical supply curve shows supply that is…
questions.why: The quantity supplied stays the same whatever the price, so PES = 0.

long.q: The price of a good rises from $8 to $10 and the quantity supplied rises from 400 to 460 units. Calculate the price elasticity of supply, state whether supply is elastic or inelastic, and explain one factor that could make supply more elastic.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity supplied = 60 ÷ 400 × 100 = 15%; % change in price = 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25%
B1: inelastic (less than 1)
B1: a factor, e.g. spare capacity / large inventories / a longer time period / resources easily moved between uses

long.q: Define price elasticity of supply.
scheme: B1: a measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied
B1: to a change in the product's price

long.q:
Extract: When the price of a toy rose from $20 to $25, a factory increased its monthly output from 8000 to 12 000 toys.
Calculate the price elasticity of supply of the toy.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity supplied = 4000 ÷ 8000 × 100 = 50%; % change in price = 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%
A1: PES = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 (elastic)

long.q: Analyse why the supply of manufactured goods is often more price elastic than the supply of agricultural products.
scheme: B1: factories can often add shifts or run machines longer when price rises
B1: and may hold stocks of finished goods that can be released quickly
B1: so the quantity supplied responds strongly to price: supply is elastic
B1: crops and animals take months or years to grow
B1: and output depends on weather and land, which farmers cannot quickly change
B1: so in the short run farm supply responds little to price: supply is inelastic

long.q:
Extract: Governments around the world are encouraging wind power. Demand for wind turbines has risen by 40% in two years. Turbine makers say they are working at full capacity, and building a new factory takes about two years.
Discuss whether the rise in demand for wind turbines will lead mainly to a rise in price or a rise in output.
scheme: B1: when demand rises, the effect on price and output depends on the PES
B1: makers are at full capacity, so in the short run supply is price inelastic
B1: so the rise in demand mainly raises the price of turbines, with little increase in output
B1: higher prices and profits give firms an incentive to expand
B1: in the long run new factories (taking about two years) make supply more elastic
B1: so over time output rises more and the price rise slows or reverses
B1: new firms may enter, and component suppliers may expand, increasing supply further
B1: justified conclusion: in the short run mainly a rise in price; in the long run mainly a rise in output, as supply becomes more elastic

questions.q: In a market economic system, resources are mainly owned by…
questions.why: A market economy relies on private ownership, with resources allocated through the price mechanism.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a market economic system?
o: Merit goods are always provided in full
Consumer choice and the profit motive encourage efficiency and innovation
Public goods are supplied by private firms
questions.why: Competition for consumers' spending pushes firms to cut costs and develop new products.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of a market economic system?
o: Firms have an incentive to cut costs
Consumers have a wide choice of products
Large inequalities of income and wealth may develop
questions.why: Goods go to those able to pay, so people with low incomes may miss out and inequality can grow.

questions.q: Consumer sovereignty means that…
o: the government decides what consumers need
consumers' spending decides what firms produce
consumers own the firms they buy from
consumers set the prices of goods
questions.why: In a market economy, firms produce what consumers choose to buy, because that is where profit lies.

questions.q: Which feature is most associated with a market economic system?
questions.why: Private firms compete for customers; the other options are features of a planned economy.

long.q: Define a market economic system.
scheme: B1: an economic system in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism (demand and supply)
B1: with mainly private ownership of resources and little government intervention

long.q:
Extract: In Freeland almost all firms are privately owned and the government rarely intervenes. Shops offer over 40 models of smartphone and new firms open every week. However, 18% of households say they cannot afford health care, and the richest 10% earn half of all income.
Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of a market economic system shown in the extract.
scheme: B1: advantage: wide consumer choice (over 40 smartphone models) / new firms entering (competition)
B1: disadvantage: inequality (the richest 10% earn half of income) / 18% of households cannot afford health care

long.q: Explain two advantages of a market economic system.
scheme: B1: one advantage, e.g. firms respond to consumer demand (consumer sovereignty)
B1: explained: resources go to the goods consumers want most, so less is wasted
B1: a second advantage, e.g. competition and the profit motive encourage efficiency and innovation / wide choice / no costly planning bureaucracy
B1: explained, e.g. firms that cut costs and develop new products earn more profit, so quality improves and prices fall

long.q: Analyse how the profit motive in a market economic system can lead to both efficient and harmful outcomes.
scheme: B1: firms aim to make as much profit as possible
B1: so they try to cut costs, using resources efficiently
B1: and they develop new products that consumers want, which increases choice
B1: however, profit can be raised by ignoring external costs such as pollution
B1: firms may not produce public goods or enough merit goods, as they cannot make a profit from them
B1: and firms with monopoly power may raise prices and restrict output to increase profit

long.q:
Extract: In Freeland almost all firms are privately owned and the government rarely intervenes. Shops offer over 40 models of smartphone and new firms open every week. However, 18% of households say they cannot afford health care, and the richest 10% earn half of all income.
Discuss whether a market economic system is the best way to allocate resources.
scheme: B1: markets respond quickly to consumer demand through the price mechanism
B1: application: Freeland offers over 40 smartphone models, showing wide choice
B1: competition and new firms encourage efficiency, innovation and lower prices
B1: however, markets allocate goods by ability to pay, so inequality can be large
B1: application: the richest 10% earn half of income and 18% cannot afford health care
B1: markets fail to provide public goods and under-provide merit goods such as health care
B1: external costs such as pollution are ignored, and monopolies may develop
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. markets are good at allocating most consumer goods, but a mixed economy with government provision of health care and public goods is likely to be better overall

questions.q: A merit good is…
o: beneficial and underconsumed in a free market
questions.why: Examples are education and healthcare; people underestimate their benefits.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a public good?
questions.why: Street lighting is non-rival and non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting.

questions.q: A public good is non-excludable. This means that…
o: it is always provided by the government
one person's use reduces the amount available to others
people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting
it has no cost of production
questions.why: Because non-payers cannot be excluded, people can be free riders, so private firms cannot charge for it.

questions.q: A factory pollutes a river, harming fishermen downstream. The harm to the fishermen is…
questions.why: The cost falls on a third party who is not part of the factory's decision, so it is an external cost.

questions.q: The private cost of producing a tonne of chemicals is $400 and the external cost is $150. What is the social cost?
questions.why: Social cost = private cost + external cost = $400 + $150 = $550.

long.q: Explain why a free market may under-provide a merit good such as education, and one way a government could correct this.
scheme: B1: consumers underestimate the benefits to themselves (lack of information)
B1: and ignore the external benefits to others, e.g. a more productive workforce
B1: so demand and consumption are below the socially best level
B1: a correction, e.g. provide it free through state schools / subsidise it / make it compulsory / give information

long.q: Define market failure.
scheme: B1: a situation in which the market (price mechanism)
B1: fails to allocate resources efficiently, so society's welfare is not maximised

long.q:
Extract: A coal-fired power station has private costs of $60 per megawatt-hour (MWh) of electricity. Air pollution from the station creates external costs of $25 per MWh. Consumers pay $70 per MWh.
Calculate the social cost per MWh and state whether society gains from producing this electricity, assuming no external benefits.
scheme: B1: social cost = $60 + $25 = $85 per MWh
B1: the social cost ($85) is greater than the benefit ($70), so society loses: too much is produced

long.q: Analyse why a free market would not provide a public good such as national defence.
scheme: B1: national defence is non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting
B1: so people have an incentive to be free riders and not pay
B1: it is also non-rival: one person being protected does not reduce protection for others
B1: private firms cannot charge enough people to cover their costs
B1: so there is no profit and the firms will not supply it
B1: this is market failure, so the government must provide it, funded by taxes

long.q: Discuss whether a free market will always lead to the over-consumption of demerit goods such as sugary drinks.
scheme: B1: a demerit good is one that is more harmful than consumers realise
B1: consumers underestimate the harm, e.g. obesity and tooth decay, so demand is too high
B1: there are external costs, e.g. extra spending by the health service paid for by taxpayers
B1: so in a free market consumption is above the socially best level
B1: however, consumers may now be well informed about the effects of sugar
B1: many people drink only small amounts, causing little harm or external cost
B1: firms may respond to demand for healthier products, e.g. low-sugar versions
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. over-consumption is likely for heavy users with poor information, but not always; better information can reduce the problem

questions.q: A maximum price set below the equilibrium price causes…
questions.why: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the lower price.

questions.q: A government sets a maximum price on bread. Where must it be set to have an effect?
o: Anywhere, it always has an effect
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many shifted a curve to show a lower equilibrium instead of drawing a maximum price line below equilibrium.

questions.q: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. What is the most likely result?
questions.why: At the higher wage more people want to work but firms want fewer workers, so labour supply exceeds demand.

questions.q: A government places an indirect tax of $1 per pack on cigarettes. The price rises from $8.00 to $8.30. How much of the tax is paid by consumers?
questions.why: Consumers pay the rise in price, $0.30; producers pay the remaining $0.70 of the tax.

questions.q: A mixed economic system is one in which…
o: all resources are owned by the government
both the private sector and the public sector allocate resources
questions.why: A mixed economy combines the price mechanism with government provision and intervention.

long.q: Define privatisation.
scheme: B1: the transfer of ownership of firms or industries
B1: from the public sector (government) to the private sector

long.q:
Extract: The government of Sandland gives milk producers a subsidy of $0.50 per litre. Before the subsidy the price was $1.80 per litre and 2 million litres were sold each week. After it, the price fell to $1.50 per litre and sales rose to 2.4 million litres per week.
Calculate the total cost to the government of the subsidy each week after it was introduced.
scheme: M1: $0.50 × 2.4 million litres
A1: $1.2 million a week

long.q: Explain how a minimum price set above the equilibrium price affects the market for an agricultural product.
scheme: B1: the minimum price is above equilibrium, so it is binding
B1: at this price quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus
B1: farmers receive a higher price, which protects their incomes
B1: but the government may have to buy and store the surplus, which is costly, and consumers pay more

long.q:
Extract: The government of Sandland gives milk producers a subsidy of $0.50 per litre. Before the subsidy the price was $1.80 per litre and 2 million litres were sold each week. After it, the price fell to $1.50 per litre and sales rose to 2.4 million litres per week.
Analyse the effects of the milk subsidy on consumers, producers and the government.
scheme: B1: the subsidy lowers producers' costs, so the supply curve shifts to the right
B1: consumers benefit from a lower price, $1.80 down to $1.50, a gain of $0.30 per litre
B1: and consumption rises from 2 million to 2.4 million litres, e.g. better nutrition
B1: producers sell more milk and keep $0.20 of each $0.50 subsidy per litre ($1.50 + $0.50 = $2.00 received)
B1: the government pays $1.2 million a week, which has an opportunity cost
B1: it may need higher taxes or less spending elsewhere, and producers may become dependent on the subsidy

long.q: Discuss whether a government should set a maximum price on rents for housing.
scheme: B1: a maximum rent set below equilibrium makes housing more affordable for tenants
B1: it protects low-income families from very high rents, reducing poverty and homelessness
B1: it can be introduced quickly and costs the government little to run
B1: however, at the lower rent quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, causing a shortage
B1: landlords may leave the rental market or sell, reducing supply further
B1: landlords have less incentive to maintain properties, so quality falls
B1: illegal side payments or a black market may develop, and those who already rent gain most
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. rent controls help some tenants in the short term, but building more homes or giving housing benefits may be better long-term policies

questions.q: What is the main function of a central bank?
o: Issuing currency and setting interest rates
questions.why: It controls monetary policy and acts as the government's and banks' bank.

questions.q: A shop displays the price of a jacket as $45. Which function of money is shown?
questions.why: The price uses money to measure and compare the value of goods, which is its unit of account function.

questions.q: Which characteristic of money makes it easy to carry around?
questions.why: Portability means money is light and easy to carry, unlike bartering with goods such as cattle.

questions.q: Which is a function of a commercial bank?
o: Setting the official base interest rate
Managing the country's gold and foreign currency reserves
questions.why: Commercial banks accept deposits and lend; the other functions belong to the central bank.

questions.q: Money solves the problem of the double coincidence of wants because…
o: it holds its value over time
it is made of precious metal
it is generally accepted in exchange, so people do not need to find someone who has what they want and wants what they have
questions.why: As a medium of exchange, money removes the need for each trader to want exactly what the other has, as barter requires.

long.q: Define money.
scheme: B1: anything that is generally acceptable
B1: as a means of payment for goods and services / settling debts

long.q: Identify two functions of money.
scheme: B1: one function, e.g. medium of exchange / unit of account
B1: a second function, e.g. store of value / standard for deferred payment

long.q: Explain two characteristics that a good form of money should have.
scheme: B1: one characteristic, e.g. acceptability
B1: explained: people must be willing to take it in exchange for goods and services
B1: a second characteristic, e.g. durability / divisibility / portability / limited supply (scarcity) / hard to forge
B1: explained, e.g. divisibility allows small and large payments to be made exactly

long.q:
Extract: In Tradeland, 70% of payments are now made by mobile phone. Commercial banks offer savings accounts paying 3% interest and approve small business loans through apps within a day. Bank lending to firms rose by 15% last year.
Analyse the role of commercial banks in Tradeland's economy.
scheme: B1: commercial banks accept deposits, giving households and firms a safe place to keep money
B1: paying 3% interest rewards saving, so households save more
B1: banks lend these savings to households and firms
B1: application: business lending rose 15%, financing investment in capital, so firms can expand and create jobs
B1: banks provide payment services such as mobile apps, making buying and selling quicker and cheaper
B1: banks profit from charging a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, which keeps them providing these services

long.q: Discuss whether the central bank is more important to an economy than commercial banks.
scheme: B1: the central bank issues the currency, so people can trust the money they use
B1: it sets interest rates (monetary policy), affecting inflation and growth across the whole economy
B1: it is the lender of last resort, preventing bank collapses in a crisis
B1: it acts as the government's bank and manages foreign currency reserves
B1: however, commercial banks deal directly with households and firms
B1: they provide the loans that finance most investment and spending, and the payment systems used every day
B1: the two depend on each other: interest-rate changes work only through commercial banks' lending
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. the central bank is more important for stability, but the economy cannot function without commercial banks, so neither is enough alone

questions.q: A household has a disposable income of $3000 a month and spends $2400. What percentage of its disposable income does it save?
Which is most likely to encourage households to borrow more?
questions.why: Lower interest rates make loans cheaper to repay, so households borrow more for items such as cars and homes.

questions.q: Compared with high-income households, low-income households usually spend…
o: a larger proportion of their income on necessities such as food
a smaller proportion of their income
questions.why: Necessities take up a large share of a small income, leaving little for luxuries or saving.

questions.q: Which is most likely to reduce household spending?
o: A rise in house prices, increasing wealth
questions.why: Higher income tax reduces disposable income, so households have less to spend.

questions.q: Why do young adults often borrow more than older people?
o: They usually have the highest incomes
They expect their incomes to rise and need to buy homes and durable goods
Banks charge them lower interest rates
questions.why: Young adults borrow against expected future income to buy items such as homes, cars and furniture.

long.q: Explain two factors that influence how much a household saves.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. the level of income
B1: explained, e.g. higher-income households can save more after paying for necessities
B1: a second factor, e.g. the rate of interest / confidence about the future / age / availability of saving schemes
B1: explained, e.g. a higher interest rate rewards saving, so households save more

long.q: Define saving.
scheme: B1: the part of disposable income that is not spent on consumption
B1: over a period of time, e.g. money placed in a bank account

long.q:
Extract: Household A has a disposable income of $2000 a month and spends $1900. Household B has a disposable income of $8000 a month and spends $6000.
Calculate the percentage of disposable income saved by each household.
scheme: B1: Household A saves $100: 100 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 5%

long.q:
Extract: Household A has a disposable income of $2000 a month and spends $1900. Household B has a disposable income of $8000 a month and spends $6000.
Analyse why high-income households such as Household B save a larger proportion of their income than low-income households such as Household A.
scheme: B1: low-income households must spend most of their income on necessities such as food, rent and transport
B1: application: Household A spends $1900 of $2000, leaving only 5% to save
B1: once necessities are paid for, extra income can be spent on luxuries or saved
B1: high-income households have more left after necessities, so they can save more
B1: application: Household B saves 25% of its income
B1: high earners may also save to buy assets or earn interest, and have more access to saving schemes

long.q: Discuss whether a rise in interest rates will reduce household spending.
scheme: B1: higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive
B1: so households buy fewer items on credit, e.g. cars, furniture, holidays
B1: households with mortgages pay more each month, leaving less disposable income
B1: saving becomes more rewarding, so households save more and spend less
B1: however, households with savings and no debt receive more interest income and may spend more
B1: spending on necessities such as food changes little whatever the interest rate
B1: if confidence is high and incomes are rising, spending may continue to grow
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. spending is likely to fall, especially on items bought on credit and for indebted households, but the effect depends on the size of the rise and household debt

questions.q: Division of labour means…
questions.why: Specialisation raises productivity but can make work repetitive.

questions.q: Which is a non-wage factor that influences a worker's choice of occupation?
o: Job security and length of holidays
questions.why: Non-wage factors are benefits other than pay, such as security, holidays, working conditions and promotion prospects.

questions.q: In a free labour market, the wage of electricians will rise if…
o: demand for electricians rises while supply is unchanged
questions.why: Higher demand for labour with unchanged supply creates a shortage, pushing the wage up.

questions.q: Why are surgeons usually paid more than cleaners?
o: The supply of surgeons is low compared with demand, because long training is needed
questions.why: Few people have the skills and qualifications needed, so the supply of surgeons is limited and their wage is high.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of specialisation for workers?
o: Work may become repetitive and boring
Workers become more skilled at their task
Less time is wasted moving between tasks
questions.why: Doing the same task repeatedly can reduce motivation and makes workers less occupationally mobile.

long.q: Explain two reasons why some workers earn more than others.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. differences in skills, qualifications and training
B1: explained, e.g. skilled workers are scarce (low supply) and more productive, so firms pay more
B1: a second reason, e.g. demand for the product they make / trade union strength / discrimination / working conditions / public or private sector
B1: explained with its effect on demand for or supply of the labour

long.q: Define the division of labour.
scheme: B1: breaking down the production process into separate tasks
B1: with each worker specialising in one task

long.q:
Extract: In Metroland, average annual earnings are $90 000 for software engineers and $24 000 for retail assistants.
Calculate how much more a software engineer earns than a retail assistant, as a percentage of a retail assistant's earnings.
Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of specialisation (division of labour) for firms.
scheme: B1: workers become more skilled at their task through repetition
B1: so output per worker (productivity) rises
B1: so average costs fall, allowing lower prices or higher profits
B1: however, repetitive work may bore workers, reducing quality and raising absence and staff turnover
B1: if one stage of production stops, e.g. through absence, the whole process may stop
B1: workers with narrow skills are less flexible, making it harder to move them to other tasks

long.q: Discuss whether a worker should always choose the job with the highest wage.
scheme: B1: a higher wage gives more income to spend and save, raising living standards
B1: it may also show the job is valued and lead to higher pensions
B1: for workers with debts or families to support, income may be the main concern
B1: however, non-wage factors also matter, e.g. job security, holidays and working hours
B1: the highest-paid job may involve stress, danger or long travel
B1: promotion prospects and training may give higher earnings in future
B1: job satisfaction and the chance to help others matter to many workers
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. the wage is important, but the worker should consider the whole package of wage and non-wage factors, so the highest-paid job is not always the best choice

questions.q: A trade union is…
o: an organisation of workers that aims to protect and improve its members' pay and working conditions
a group of firms that agree to fix prices
a government department that sets wages
a bank owned by its workers
questions.why: Trade unions represent workers in dealings with employers and the government.

questions.q: Collective bargaining means…
o: each worker negotiating alone with the employer
the union negotiating with employers on behalf of its members
the government setting wages for all workers
workers buying shares in their firm
questions.why: The union negotiates for the whole group of workers, which gives it more power than individuals have.

questions.q: Which is most likely to increase a trade union's bargaining power?
o: Workers who can easily be replaced
High demand for the product the workers make
questions.why: When demand for the product is high, the firm has more to lose from a strike and can afford higher wages.

questions.q: Which is an example of industrial action?
questions.why: Industrial action is action by workers, such as strikes or working strictly to rule, to put pressure on employers.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage to a firm of a strong trade union?
o: Higher wage costs that may raise prices and reduce competitiveness
questions.why: Higher wages increase costs, which can reduce profits or force higher prices.

long.q: Define a trade union.
scheme: B1: an organisation of workers
B1: that aims to protect and improve its members' pay, working conditions and job security

long.q:
Extract: The Union of Bus Drivers in Portcity represents 85% of the city's bus drivers. It is asking for an 8% pay rise. Inflation is 5% and the bus company's profits rose by 20% last year. The union has said its members will strike if the offer is too low.
Identify two pieces of evidence that the union is in a strong bargaining position.
scheme: B1: it represents 85% of bus drivers (high membership)
B1: the company's profits rose 20%, so it can afford a pay rise / the union can threaten a strike

long.q: Explain two benefits to a worker of joining a trade union.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. higher wages through collective bargaining
B1: explained: the union negotiates for all members together, so it has more power than one worker
B1: a second benefit, e.g. better working conditions and health and safety / protection against unfair dismissal / legal advice / training
B1: explained, e.g. the union can represent a worker in a dispute with the employer

long.q:
Extract: The Union of Bus Drivers in Portcity represents 85% of the city's bus drivers. It is asking for an 8% pay rise. Inflation is 5% and the bus company's profits rose by 20% last year. The union has said its members will strike if the offer is too low.
Analyse the possible effects of a strike by the bus drivers on the bus company and on the wider economy of Portcity.
scheme: B1: the company loses fare revenue during the strike while some costs, e.g. vehicles and buildings, continue
B1: so its profits fall and its reputation may suffer, with some passengers switching permanently to cars or taxis
B1: the drivers lose wages during the strike
B1: workers who rely on buses may be late or unable to reach work
B1: so firms in Portcity lose output and shops lose customers
B1: if the strike wins an 8% rise, the company's costs rise and fares may increase

long.q: Discuss whether trade unions benefit an economy.
scheme: B1: unions can raise wages and improve working conditions for members
B1: this may increase spending in the economy and reduce poverty
B1: better conditions and training can raise productivity and reduce staff turnover
B1: unions provide a channel of communication between workers and managers
B1: however, wage rises above productivity growth increase firms' costs
B1: this can lead to higher prices, less competitiveness and unemployment
B1: strikes lose output and disrupt other firms and consumers
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. unions benefit the economy when they negotiate cooperatively and link pay to productivity, but frequent strikes or excessive wage demands can harm it

questions.q: As a supermarket chain grows, it buys goods in bulk at a lower price per unit. This is an example of…
questions.why: Bulk buying lowers average cost because of the firm's own growth, so it is an internal purchasing economy of scale.

questions.q: A car manufacturer merges with a firm that makes tyres. This is a…
questions.why: The car maker joins with its supplier at an earlier stage of production, so it is backward vertical integration.

questions.q: A firm that catches fish is in which sector of the economy?
questions.why: The primary sector extracts natural resources, including fishing, farming and mining.

questions.q: As a firm grows very large, communication between departments becomes slow and average costs start to rise. This is an example of…
questions.why: Diseconomies of scale are rises in average cost caused by a firm becoming too large to manage efficiently.

questions.q: Which is a reason small firms survive alongside large firms?
o: They find it easier to borrow money
They gain the most from economies of scale
They can offer a personal service and serve small (niche) markets
questions.why: Small firms can give personal attention and supply markets too small to interest large firms.

long.q: Apart from buying in bulk, explain two internal economies of scale that a large car manufacturer could benefit from.
scheme: B1: one economy, e.g. technical: using large, specialised machinery and production lines
B1: explained: the cost of the machinery is spread over many cars, so the average cost falls
B1: a second economy, e.g. financial (borrowing at lower interest) / managerial (specialist managers) / marketing (advertising cost spread over more sales) / risk-bearing
B1: explained with how it lowers average cost

long.q: Define a horizontal merger.
scheme: B1: the joining of two (or more) firms
B1: at the same stage of production in the same industry

long.q:
Extract: FreshCo, a supermarket chain, has bought FarmPure, a group of dairy farms, and ValueMart, a rival supermarket chain. FreshCo now buys in much larger quantities and its average costs have fallen by 8%. However, managers report that decisions now take longer and staff morale has fallen.
Identify the type of merger when FreshCo bought FarmPure and when it bought ValueMart.
scheme: B1: FarmPure: backward vertical merger
B1: ValueMart: horizontal merger

long.q:
Extract: FreshCo, a supermarket chain, has bought FarmPure, a group of dairy farms, and ValueMart, a rival supermarket chain. FreshCo now buys in much larger quantities and its average costs have fallen by 8%. However, managers report that decisions now take longer and staff morale has fallen.
Analyse why FreshCo's average costs fell and why it may now face diseconomies of scale.
scheme: B1: buying in larger quantities gives purchasing economies of scale (bulk-buying discounts)
B1: owning dairy farms removes the supplier's profit margin and secures supplies
B1: so FreshCo's average costs fell by 8%
B1: however, a much larger firm is harder to manage and coordinate
B1: application: decisions now take longer and staff morale has fallen
B1: slow decisions and less motivated staff reduce efficiency, so average costs may start to rise

long.q: Discuss whether small firms will always find it hard to compete with large firms.
scheme: B1: large firms gain economies of scale, so they have lower average costs and can charge lower prices
B1: large firms can borrow more cheaply and spend more on advertising and research
B1: small firms may struggle to raise finance and face higher costs per unit
B1: however, small firms can offer a personal, flexible service
B1: they can serve niche markets that are too small for large firms
B1: they may avoid diseconomies of scale and make decisions quickly
B1: governments may help small firms, e.g. with grants or lower taxes, and the internet lets them reach wide markets cheaply
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. small firms find it hard to compete on price in mass markets, but not always: they can succeed where personal service, local knowledge or flexibility matter

questions.q: Productivity is…
o: the total output of a firm
output per unit of input, e.g. per worker per hour
the total revenue of a firm
questions.why: Productivity measures efficiency: how much is produced by each unit of a factor of production.

questions.q: A factory with 20 workers produces 1200 units a day. After training, the same 20 workers produce 1500 units a day. By how much has labour productivity increased?
questions.why: Productivity rises from 1200 ÷ 20 = 60 to 1500 ÷ 20 = 75 units per worker, an increase of 15.

questions.q: Which production method is most likely to be capital-intensive?
questions.why: Capital-intensive production uses a high proportion of machinery relative to labour.

questions.q: Why might a firm choose labour-intensive production?
o: It wants to mass-produce identical items
Labour is cheap relative to capital
questions.why: Where wages are low compared with the cost of machines, using more workers is the lower-cost method.

questions.q: The demand for factors of production is a derived demand. This means that…
