o: it depends on the demand for the products the factors help to make
it is set by the government
it depends only on interest rates
questions.why: Firms want workers and machines only because consumers want the goods and services they produce.

long.q: Define productivity.
scheme: B1: the output produced
B1: per unit of input over a period of time, e.g. output per worker per hour

long.q:
Extract: BrightShirts is a clothing factory. In 2024, 50 workers produced 40 000 shirts. In 2025, after new sewing machines were installed, 60 workers produced 54 000 shirts.
Calculate the change in labour productivity at BrightShirts between 2024 and 2025.
scheme: M1: 2024: 40 000 ÷ 50 = 800 shirts per worker; 2025: 54 000 ÷ 60 = 900 shirts per worker
A1: an increase of 100 shirts per worker per year (12.5%)

long.q: Explain two influences on a firm's demand for a factor of production.
scheme: B1: one influence, e.g. the demand for the product the factor helps to make (derived demand)
B1: explained: if sales of the product rise, the firm needs more workers and machines
B1: a second influence, e.g. the price of the factor compared with other factors / the productivity of the factor
B1: explained, e.g. if wages rise relative to the cost of machines, the firm demands less labour and more capital

long.q:
Extract: BrightShirts is a clothing factory. In 2024, 50 workers produced 40 000 shirts. In 2025, after new sewing machines were installed, 60 workers produced 54 000 shirts.
Analyse how BrightShirts could increase its labour productivity further.
scheme: B1: training workers improves their skills
B1: so each worker can produce more shirts per hour, with fewer mistakes
B1: investing in more or better machinery (as in 2025) lets each worker produce more
B1: further specialisation (division of labour) lets workers become faster at single tasks
B1: better motivation, e.g. bonuses linked to output, may encourage workers to work harder
B1: higher productivity lowers average costs, so BrightShirts can cut prices or earn more profit

long.q: Discuss whether a firm should replace workers with machines (become more capital-intensive).
scheme: B1: machines can work for long hours without breaks, raising output and productivity
B1: they often produce goods of consistent quality
B1: in the long run average costs may fall, making the firm more competitive
B1: however, machines are expensive to buy, maintain and repair
B1: if wages are low, labour-intensive production may be cheaper
B1: workers are more flexible and better for personal or hand-made products
B1: job losses may lower morale and bring opposition from trade unions
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. switching is sensible for large-scale, standardised production where wages are high, but not for small firms or services that need a personal touch

questions.q: Total revenue is…
questions.why: Profit = total revenue − total cost.

questions.q: A firm produces 200 units. Its fixed costs are $1 000 and its total variable costs are $600. What is its average total cost?
questions.why: Average total cost = total cost ÷ output = (1 000 + 600) ÷ 200 = $8.

questions.q: Which is a fixed cost for a bakery?
o: Electricity used to bake each batch
questions.why: Rent stays the same however many loaves are baked; the others rise with output, so they are variable costs.

questions.q: A firm sells 400 units and earns total revenue of $6000. What is its average revenue?
questions.why: Average revenue = total revenue ÷ quantity sold = 6000 ÷ 400 = $15, which equals the price per unit.

questions.q: A social enterprise sets low prices so that more poor families can afford its water filters. What is its main objective?
questions.why: Its aim is to benefit society rather than to make as much profit as possible.

long.q: A firm has fixed costs of $600. It makes 150 units with total variable costs of $900 and sells each unit for $12. Calculate its total cost, its average total cost and its profit.
scheme: B1: average total cost = 1500 ÷ 150 = $10
M1: total revenue = 150 × 12 = $1800

long.q: Define variable cost.
scheme: B1: a cost that changes directly with the level of output
B1: e.g. raw materials; it is zero when output is zero

long.q:
Extract: PrintFast has fixed costs of $2000 a month. Each poster has a variable cost of $3 and sells for $8.
Calculate the change in PrintFast's average fixed cost when its output rises from 500 to 1000 posters a month.
scheme: A1: average fixed cost falls by $2 per poster

long.q:
Extract: TechNova is a new firm selling home security cameras. It has set its prices below those of its rivals to win customers, and it made a loss in its first year. Its owners say their aim is to survive and build market share.
Analyse why a new firm such as TechNova might aim for survival or growth rather than profit maximisation.
scheme: B1: a new firm has no customers or reputation and faces established rivals
B1: so its first aim is to survive, covering its costs and not running out of money
B1: application: TechNova made a loss in its first year, so surviving is its priority
B1: low prices attract customers away from rivals, increasing market share
B1: as it grows it may gain economies of scale, lowering average costs
B1: so it can earn higher profits in the long run, even though short-run profit is sacrificed

long.q: Discuss whether profit maximisation is the most important objective for a firm.
scheme: B1: profit is the reward for enterprise and risk
B1: profits can be reinvested in new capital and research, helping the firm to grow
B1: shareholders expect high profits, and firms that make losses may close
B1: however, a new firm may put survival first
B1: other firms aim for growth or market share, accepting lower profit now for higher profit later
B1: social enterprises and public-sector organisations aim for social welfare
B1: firms that chase profit at the expense of customers, workers or the environment may lose their reputation
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. profit matters to most private firms in the long run, but the most important objective depends on the firm's age, ownership and market position

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of a monopoly?
o: A single seller protected by high barriers to entry
Identical products sold by many firms
questions.why: A monopoly is a market with one main supplier, and barriers stop new firms from entering.

questions.q: Which is a barrier to entry into a market?
o: A patent held by the existing firm
Many small firms in the market
questions.why: A patent gives the holder the legal right to be the only producer of a product for a period of time.

questions.q: In a highly competitive market, firms are likely to…
o: charge high prices with no fear of losing customers
earn high long-run profits protected by barriers
have little control over the price they charge
questions.why: With many rivals selling similar products, a firm that raises its price will lose customers.

questions.q: Which is a likely benefit to consumers of a competitive market?
questions.why: Firms compete for customers by cutting prices, improving quality and offering more choice.

questions.q: A firm sells 85% of all the products in its market. This indicates…
o: a high degree of monopoly power
that there are no barriers to entry
that the firm is a price taker
questions.why: A very large market share gives the firm power to influence price and output.

long.q: Discuss whether a monopoly is always bad for consumers.
scheme: B1: a reason it may be bad, e.g. higher prices because there are no close substitutes
B1: explained, e.g. the monopolist restricts output to raise price and profit
B1: a second disadvantage, e.g. less choice / lower quality / less pressure to be efficient
B1: a reason it may be good, e.g. economies of scale can lower average costs and prices
B1: a second advantage, e.g. high profits fund research and new products / avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly)
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. depends on whether it is regulated and whether cost savings are passed on

long.q: Define a monopoly.
scheme: B1: a market with a single (or dominant) supplier
B1: protected by high barriers to entry, with no close substitutes

long.q:
Extract: In Islandia, RailOne is the only train operator. It holds a 30-year government licence, and building a rival rail network would cost about $10 billion. In the capital city, more than 300 small cafés compete for customers, and a new café can open for about $50 000.
Identify two barriers to entry in Islandia's rail market.
scheme: B1: the 30-year government licence held by RailOne (legal barrier)
B1: the very high cost (about $10 billion) of building a rival network

long.q: Explain two features of a competitive market.
scheme: B1: one feature, e.g. many buyers and sellers
B1: explained: no single firm can control the market price
B1: a second feature, e.g. low or no barriers to entry / similar products / good information for buyers
B1: explained, e.g. if profits are high, new firms enter, increasing supply and pushing prices down

long.q:
Extract: In Islandia, RailOne is the only train operator. It holds a 30-year government licence, and building a rival rail network would cost about $10 billion. In the capital city, more than 300 small cafés compete for customers, and a new café can open for about $50 000.
Discuss whether consumers are better off in Islandia's café market than in its rail market.
scheme: B1: the café market is competitive, with over 300 cafés and low entry costs of about $50 000
B1: so cafés must keep prices low and quality high or lose customers to rivals
B1: consumers have wide choice, and new cafés bring new ideas
B1: RailOne is a monopoly, so it can raise fares and has less pressure to improve service
B1: however, a single rail network avoids wasteful duplication of very costly track (natural monopoly)
B1: RailOne may gain economies of scale and use profits to invest in new trains
B1: the government can regulate RailOne's fares and service standards as part of the licence
B1: justified conclusion, e.g. consumers are generally better off in the café market, but a well-regulated rail monopoly may serve them better than several competing networks

questions.q: Which is an example of the government acting as a producer?
o: A state-owned railway company running train services
A law banning smoking in restaurants
A central bank publishing inflation figures
questions.why: As a producer the government supplies goods and services itself, often through state-owned enterprises.

questions.q: A government passes a law setting minimum safety standards that all factories must meet. Which role is it performing?
questions.why: Setting and enforcing rules on how firms operate is the government's role as a regulator.

questions.q: Which is an example of a government's international role?
o: Negotiating a free trade agreement with another country
questions.why: Internationally, governments make trade agreements and work with other countries and international organisations.

questions.q: In a country, 18% of all workers are teachers, nurses, soldiers and civil servants paid by the state. This mainly shows the government's role as…
questions.why: The public sector employs a large share of workers, so government decisions affect employment directly.

questions.q: Which service is most likely to be provided by local government rather than national government?
o: Deciding the country's exchange rate policy
Representing the country at the World Trade Organization
questions.why: Local government provides services for a town or region, such as refuse collection, local roads and parks.

long.q: Extract: In Country Zarel the government owns the national electricity company and employs 2.4 million of the 12 million people in the labour force. Local councils run refuse collection and parks. This year the government joined a regional trade agreement and introduced new rules limiting the smoke that factories may release. Define 'public sector'.
scheme: B1: the part of the economy owned or controlled by the government
B1: e.g. providing goods and services such as state schools or state-owned enterprises, financed largely by taxes

long.q: Extract: In Country Zarel the government owns the national electricity company and employs 2.4 million of the 12 million people in the labour force. Local councils run refuse collection and parks. This year the government joined a regional trade agreement and introduced new rules limiting the smoke that factories may release. Calculate the percentage of Zarel's labour force employed by the government.

Extract: In Country Zarel the government owns the national electricity company and employs 2.4 million of the 12 million people in the labour force. Local councils run refuse collection and parks. This year the government joined a regional trade agreement and introduced new rules limiting the smoke that factories may release. Explain two reasons why a government may choose to run the electricity industry itself rather than leave it to private firms.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. electricity is a natural monopoly
B1: explained: a private monopoly might charge high prices and restrict output to make high profits
B1: a second reason, e.g. to make sure every area, including remote and poor ones, is supplied / it is a strategic industry
B1: explained: a private firm may not supply areas where it cannot make a profit, but households and firms everywhere need power

long.q: Extract: In Country Zarel the government owns the national electricity company and employs 2.4 million of the 12 million people in the labour force. Local councils run refuse collection and parks. This year the government joined a regional trade agreement and introduced new rules limiting the smoke that factories may release. Analyse how the new rules limiting smoke from factories may affect firms and the wider economy in Zarel.
scheme: B1: the rules force firms to reduce pollution, a negative externality
B1: firms must buy cleaner equipment or change methods, so their costs of production rise
B1: higher costs reduce supply, so prices rise and output may fall
B1: some firms may cut jobs or become less competitive against foreign firms without such rules
B1: third parties benefit: cleaner air means fewer health problems and lower healthcare costs
B1: firms may be pushed to develop cleaner, more efficient technology, raising productivity in the long run

long.q: Extract: In Country Zarel the government owns the national electricity company and employs 2.4 million of the 12 million people in the labour force. Local councils run refuse collection and parks. This year the government joined a regional trade agreement and introduced new rules limiting the smoke that factories may release. Discuss whether Zarel's government should keep ownership of the national electricity company or sell it to the private sector.
scheme: B1: keep: the government can keep prices affordable for households and firms
B1: keep: it can guarantee supply to all regions and protect a strategic industry
B1: keep: any profits go to the government and can fund public services
B1: sell: private owners seeking profit have an incentive to cut costs and improve efficiency
B1: sell: the government receives revenue from the sale, which could reduce borrowing
B1: sell: private firms may invest more and face less political interference
B1: evaluation: depends on whether a privatised firm would be a monopoly and how well it is regulated
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. keep it public unless a strong regulator can control prices after a sale

questions.q: Which is a macroeconomic aim of government?
questions.why: Aims include growth, low unemployment, stable prices, a sustainable balance of payments and fair income distribution.

questions.q: Which pair of macroeconomic aims is most likely to conflict in the short run?
o: Economic growth and higher tax revenue
questions.why: Raising demand to create jobs can push up prices, so reducing unemployment may increase inflation.

questions.q: A government cuts income tax to boost economic growth. Which problem is most likely to arise for another of its aims?
o: The current account may worsen as households buy more imports
questions.why: Higher disposable income raises spending, part of which goes on imports, so growth can conflict with balance of payments stability.

questions.q: Why might a government aim for a more equal distribution of income?
o: To widen the gap between rich and poor
To raise the general price level
To increase the current account deficit
questions.why: Redistribution, for example through progressive taxes and benefits, narrows inequality and reduces relative poverty.

questions.q: In a year a country's real GDP rose by 4%, unemployment fell from 6% to 4% and inflation rose from 2% to 7%. What does this show?
o: Progress on growth and employment came with a conflict with stable prices
The government achieved all its macroeconomic aims
The economy was in a recession
questions.why: Growth and lower unemployment were achieved, but inflation moved further from a low, stable rate.

long.q: Extract: In Country Mirava in 2025 real GDP grew by 5.5%, unemployment fell from 7.0% to 4.5% and inflation rose from 2.0% to 6.5%. The current account deficit widened from 1% to 4% of GDP. The government's targets are inflation of 2% and a current account close to balance. Define 'economic growth'.
scheme: B1: an increase in real GDP / in the output of goods and services
B1: over a period of time / an increase in the economy's productive capacity

long.q: Extract: In Country Mirava in 2025 real GDP grew by 5.5%, unemployment fell from 7.0% to 4.5% and inflation rose from 2.0% to 6.5%. The current account deficit widened from 1% to 4% of GDP. The government's targets are inflation of 2% and a current account close to balance. Using the data, identify two macroeconomic aims on which Mirava's performance improved in 2025.
scheme: B1: economic growth: real GDP rose by 5.5%
B1: low unemployment: unemployment fell from 7.0% to 4.5%

long.q: Extract: In Country Mirava in 2025 real GDP grew by 5.5%, unemployment fell from 7.0% to 4.5% and inflation rose from 2.0% to 6.5%. The current account deficit widened from 1% to 4% of GDP. The government's targets are inflation of 2% and a current account close to balance. Explain two reasons why a government aims for price stability.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. inflation reduces the purchasing power of money
B1: explained: people on fixed incomes and savers become worse off, so living standards fall
B1: a second reason, e.g. high inflation makes exports less price competitive / creates uncertainty for firms
B1: explained: export sales fall, or firms delay investment because future costs and prices are hard to predict

long.q: Extract: In Country Mirava in 2025 real GDP grew by 5.5%, unemployment fell from 7.0% to 4.5% and inflation rose from 2.0% to 6.5%. The current account deficit widened from 1% to 4% of GDP. The government's targets are inflation of 2% and a current account close to balance. Analyse how the fast economic growth in Mirava may have caused both the rise in inflation and the wider current account deficit.
scheme: B1: growth driven by rising total demand / consumer spending
B1: demand rises faster than output, so firms raise prices: demand-pull inflation
B1: as unemployment falls, firms compete for scarce workers, so wages and costs rise: cost-push pressure
B1: higher incomes lead households to buy more imports
B1: higher inflation in Mirava makes its exports less price competitive and imports relatively cheaper
B1: so imports rise faster than exports, widening the current account deficit from 1% to 4% of GDP

A tax on a person's wealth

questions.q: Cutting interest rates is likely to…

Households borrow more to buy cars

questions.why: Payments rise from 4% × 150,000 = $6,000 to 5.5% × 150,000 = $8,250, an increase of $2,250.

questions.why: Monetary policy changes interest rates, the money supply or the exchange rate.

questions.q: Supply-side policies aim mainly to…
o: increase the productive capacity of the economy
raise total demand by cutting interest rates

They can only be used by the central bank

The government gains control of more firms
Private owners seeking profit have an incentive to cut costs
It guarantees that prices will fall

The economy moves along the PPC with no change in capacity
questions.why: Higher productivity increases the maximum output the economy can produce, shifting the PPC outwards.

a current account deficit lasting two years
a fall in the exchange rate

a fall in the value of a currency

long.q: Extract: Data for two countries in 2025. Country Arlo: real GDP per head $28,000; HDI 0.78; life expectancy 71 years; the richest 10% receive 45% of income. Country Belto: real GDP per head $19,000; HDI 0.84; life expectancy 79 years; the richest 10% receive 25% of income. Define 'Human Development Index (HDI)'.
scheme: B1: a composite measure of development / living standards, with a value between 0 and 1
B1: combining income (GNI per head), education (years of schooling) and health (life expectancy)

long.q: Extract: Data for two countries in 2025. Country Arlo: real GDP per head $28,000; HDI 0.78; life expectancy 71 years; the richest 10% receive 45% of income. Country Belto: real GDP per head $19,000; HDI 0.84; life expectancy 79 years; the richest 10% receive 25% of income. Using the data, identify two pieces of evidence that Belto may have higher living standards than Arlo despite its lower real GDP per head.
scheme: B1: Belto has a higher HDI (0.84 compared with 0.78)
B1: Belto has a longer life expectancy (79 compared with 71 years) / a more equal income distribution (25% compared with 45%)

long.q: Extract: Data for two countries in 2025. Country Arlo: real GDP per head $28,000; HDI 0.78; life expectancy 71 years; the richest 10% receive 45% of income. Country Belto: real GDP per head $19,000; HDI 0.84; life expectancy 79 years; the richest 10% receive 25% of income. Analyse why Arlo's higher real GDP per head may not mean that most of its people have a higher standard of living than people in Belto.
scheme: B1: real GDP per head is an average and says nothing about distribution
B1: in Arlo the richest 10% receive 45% of income, so income is very unequal
B1: most people in Arlo may therefore earn well below the average of $28,000
B1: Arlo's shorter life expectancy suggests poorer health care, diet or housing
B1: Arlo's lower HDI suggests weaker education and health despite higher income
B1: GDP may include output that does little for wellbeing, or come with pollution and long working hours

long.q: Extract: Data for two countries in 2025. Country Arlo: real GDP per head $28,000; HDI 0.78; life expectancy 71 years; the richest 10% receive 45% of income. Country Belto: real GDP per head $19,000; HDI 0.84; life expectancy 79 years; the richest 10% receive 25% of income. Discuss whether the HDI is a better measure of living standards than real GDP per head.
scheme: B1: for HDI: it includes health and education as well as income
B1: for HDI: it gives a broader view of wellbeing, e.g. Belto ranks above Arlo
B1: for HDI: its income measure is adjusted for differences in the cost of living (purchasing power)
B1: for GDP per head: it is simpler, published more often and easier to compare over time
B1: against HDI: like GDP per head it is an average that ignores inequality, and it leaves out freedom, environment and working hours
B1: against HDI: data on schooling may be unreliable and the weighting of the three parts is a matter of judgement
B1: evaluation: both are limited, so they are best used together with other indicators
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. the HDI is the better single measure because it covers more aspects of life, but it is not complete

questions.q: Absolute poverty means…
o: not having enough for basic needs
questions.why: Relative poverty compares income with others in the country.

questions.q: A household's income is less than half the median income in its country, but it can afford food and shelter. The household is in…
questions.why: Relative poverty means having much less than others in the same society, even if basic needs are met.

questions.q: Which policy is most likely to reduce poverty in the long run by raising people's earning power?
o: Improving access to education and training
questions.why: Better skills raise productivity, giving access to better-paid jobs.

questions.q: How can a progressive income tax combined with welfare benefits reduce inequality?
o: It takes the same share of income from everyone
It takes a higher share of income from the rich and transfers income to the poor
It raises the prices of necessities
It increases the incomes of the richest households
questions.why: Progressive taxes and benefits redistribute income from higher to lower earners.

questions.q: In a country of 60 million people, 9 million live below the national poverty line. What percentage of the population is in poverty?

long.q: Explain two causes of poverty in a developing economy.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. unemployment and underemployment / low wages
B1: explained, e.g. people have little or no income to buy basic necessities
B1: a second cause, e.g. poor education and health care / low productivity / high population growth / poor infrastructure / corruption or conflict
B1: explained with how it keeps incomes low

long.q: Discuss whether foreign aid is the best way to reduce poverty in a developing economy.
scheme: B1: aid can pay for schools, hospitals, clean water and infrastructure
B1: explained, e.g. this raises productivity and incomes in the long run
B1: a limitation, e.g. aid may be wasted through corruption / tied to buying the donor's goods / creates dependency
B1: an alternative, e.g. trade, foreign direct investment, microfinance, government policies on education or minimum wages
B1: explained with its effect on poverty
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. aid is most useful when well targeted and combined with other policies

long.q: Extract: In Country Ravena 35% of people live in rural areas where incomes depend on small-scale farming, and 22% of the population lives in absolute poverty. Primary school enrolment is 70% in rural areas and 95% in cities. The government is considering a national minimum wage and a programme to build rural schools and roads. Define 'relative poverty'.
scheme: B1: having a low income compared with others in the same country, e.g. below a set percentage of median income
B1: so that a person cannot enjoy the standard of living normal in that society

long.q: Extract: In Country Ravena 35% of people live in rural areas where incomes depend on small-scale farming, and 22% of the population lives in absolute poverty. Primary school enrolment is 70% in rural areas and 95% in cities. The government is considering a national minimum wage and a programme to build rural schools and roads. Analyse how building rural schools and roads could reduce poverty in Ravena.
scheme: B1: more rural schools would raise enrolment from 70%, so more people become literate and skilled
B1: skilled workers are more productive and can get better-paid jobs / move between occupations
B1: roads cut transport costs, so farmers can sell crops in city markets at better prices
B1: roads make it easier to reach jobs in towns, improving geographical mobility
B1: better infrastructure attracts firms to rural areas, creating employment
B1: in the long run children escape the poverty of their parents, breaking the cycle of poverty

long.q: Extract: In Country Ravena 35% of people live in rural areas where incomes depend on small-scale farming, and 22% of the population lives in absolute poverty. Primary school enrolment is 70% in rural areas and 95% in cities. The government is considering a national minimum wage and a programme to build rural schools and roads. Discuss whether introducing a national minimum wage would reduce poverty in Ravena.
scheme: B1: for: it raises the income of the lowest-paid employees, helping them afford basic needs
B1: for: it may encourage more people to look for work
B1: for: higher spending by low-paid workers raises demand for local firms
B1: against: many of Ravena's poor are self-employed small farmers, not employees, so they gain nothing
B1: against: higher labour costs may lead firms to employ fewer workers, raising unemployment
B1: against: it is hard to enforce in the informal economy
B1: against: firms may pass higher costs on in higher prices, reducing real incomes
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. it would help some urban workers, but schools and roads would do more for the rural poor

questions.q: Why does the size of a country's population not change its death rate directly?
o: Death rate is measured per 1000 of the population
Death rate is a total number
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common error was to cite population size; death rate is per 1000 people, so size cancels out.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 30 per 1000 and a death rate of 10 per 1000, with no migration. What is its rate of natural increase?
questions.why: Natural increase = 30 − 10 = 20 per 1000, which is 2% of the population a year.

questions.q: A population pyramid has a wide base that narrows quickly towards the top. What does this most likely show?
o: A high birth rate and relatively low life expectancy
An ageing population with a low birth rate
questions.why: Many young people at the base and few older people at the top is typical of a developing economy.

questions.q: Optimum population is the population at which…
o: the country's population is the largest it has ever been
output per head is highest, given the country's resources
questions.why: Below the optimum there are too few workers to use resources fully; above it, output per head falls.

questions.q: A country has 12 million people aged under 15, 8 million aged 65 and over, and 40 million aged 15–64. What is its dependency ratio (dependants per 100 people of working age)?
questions.why: Dependants = 12 + 8 = 20 million; 20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 50.

long.q: A country has a population of 50 million, a birth rate of 24 per 1000 and a death rate of 9 per 1000. Net migration is −50 000 a year. Calculate the change in its population over one year.
scheme: M1: natural increase rate = 24 − 9 = 15 per 1000
A1: population change = 750 000 − 50 000 = +700 000

long.q: Explain two consequences of an ageing population for an economy.
scheme: B1: one consequence, e.g. government spending on pensions and healthcare rises
B1: explained, e.g. taxes may need to rise or other spending be cut
B1: a second consequence, e.g. a smaller labour force / higher dependency ratio / changes in demand towards goods for older people
B1: explained, e.g. fewer workers may mean labour shortages and slower growth

long.q: Extract: Country Lumora has a population of 30 million, a birth rate of 11 per 1000, a death rate of 12 per 1000 and net migration of +40,000 a year. People aged 65 and over make up 24% of the population, up from 15% in 2005. The government is considering raising the retirement age from 62 to 67. Define 'net migration'.
scheme: B1: the difference between immigration and emigration
B1: the number of people coming to live in a country minus the number leaving it, over a period

long.q: Extract: Country Lumora has a population of 30 million, a birth rate of 11 per 1000, a death rate of 12 per 1000 and net migration of +40,000 a year. People aged 65 and over make up 24% of the population, up from 15% in 2005. The government is considering raising the retirement age from 62 to 67. Identify two pieces of evidence from the extract that Lumora has an ageing population.
scheme: B1: the share of people aged 65 and over rose from 15% to 24%
B1: the birth rate is low (11 per 1000) and below the death rate (12 per 1000)

long.q: Extract: Country Lumora has a population of 30 million, a birth rate of 11 per 1000, a death rate of 12 per 1000 and net migration of +40,000 a year. People aged 65 and over make up 24% of the population, up from 15% in 2005. The government is considering raising the retirement age from 62 to 67. Analyse how raising the retirement age from 62 to 67 could affect Lumora's economy.
scheme: B1: more people stay in the labour force, increasing the economy's productive capacity
B1: the dependency ratio falls as fewer people are retired
B1: government spending on pensions falls because people draw them later
B1: people working longer pay more income tax, raising government revenue
B1: fewer job vacancies may open for young people, raising youth unemployment
B1: some older workers may be less productive or have health problems, though they bring experience

long.q: Extract: Country Lumora has a population of 30 million, a birth rate of 11 per 1000, a death rate of 12 per 1000 and net migration of +40,000 a year. People aged 65 and over make up 24% of the population, up from 15% in 2005. The government is considering raising the retirement age from 62 to 67. Discuss whether encouraging immigration is the best way for Lumora to deal with its ageing population.
scheme: B1: for: immigrants are often of working age, increasing the labour force and filling shortages
B1: for: they pay taxes that help fund pensions and health care
B1: for: younger immigrants may raise the birth rate and bring new skills
B1: against: more people put pressure on housing, public services and infrastructure
B1: against: wages for some local workers may fall / social tensions may rise
B1: against: immigrants also grow old, so it is only a temporary solution
B1: evaluation: alternatives include raising the retirement age, encouraging a higher birth rate or raising productivity
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. immigration helps in the short run but works best combined with a higher retirement age

topics.name: Differences in economic development between countries

questions.q: Compared with a developed economy, which is most likely to be a feature of a developing economy?
o: A larger share of workers in the primary sector
A higher proportion of elderly people
questions.why: Developing economies usually rely more on agriculture and mining, while developed ones have more tertiary-sector jobs.

questions.q: Why do many developing economies have low levels of investment?
o: Low incomes mean low saving, so few funds are available to lend
They already have too many factories
questions.why: People on low incomes spend most of what they earn, leaving little saving to finance investment.

questions.q: Which is most likely to explain why labour productivity is lower in a developing economy than in a developed one?
o: Less spending on education and training
questions.why: Fewer skills and less capital per worker mean lower output per worker.

questions.q: In Country P, 60% of workers are in the primary sector, 15% in the secondary and 25% in the tertiary. In Country Q the figures are 3%, 20% and 77%. Which conclusion is most likely?
o: P is likely to be less developed than Q
P is likely to be more developed than Q
Q has more workers in manufacturing than in services
questions.why: A large primary sector is typical of a developing economy; a large tertiary sector is typical of a developed one.

questions.q: Why do developing economies often have higher population growth than developed economies?
o: Higher birth rates, partly because children help the family earn a living
questions.why: Where incomes are low and pensions rare, larger families can be a source of labour and support in old age.

long.q: Extract: Data for 2025. Country Sundra: GDP per head $2,400; 55% of workers in agriculture; saving 9% of GDP; average years of schooling 5; doctors per 1000 people 0.3; population growth 2.8% a year. Country Velmark: GDP per head $48,000; 2% of workers in agriculture; saving 22% of GDP; average years of schooling 13; doctors per 1000 people 3.5; population growth 0.2% a year. Define 'developing economy'.
scheme: B1: a country with low income / low real GDP per head
B1: and low living standards, e.g. low HDI or a large primary sector

long.q: Extract: Data for 2025. Country Sundra: GDP per head $2,400; 55% of workers in agriculture; saving 9% of GDP; average years of schooling 5; doctors per 1000 people 0.3; population growth 2.8% a year. Country Velmark: GDP per head $48,000; 2% of workers in agriculture; saving 22% of GDP; average years of schooling 13; doctors per 1000 people 3.5; population growth 0.2% a year. Calculate how many times greater GDP per head is in Velmark than in Sundra.
scheme: A1: = 20 times

long.q: Extract: Data for 2025. Country Sundra: GDP per head $2,400; 55% of workers in agriculture; saving 9% of GDP; average years of schooling 5; doctors per 1000 people 0.3; population growth 2.8% a year. Country Velmark: GDP per head $48,000; 2% of workers in agriculture; saving 22% of GDP; average years of schooling 13; doctors per 1000 people 3.5; population growth 0.2% a year. Explain two reasons why labour productivity is likely to be lower in Sundra than in Velmark.
scheme: B1: fewer years of schooling (5 compared with 13)
B1: explained: workers have fewer skills, so they produce less per hour
B1: low saving (9% of GDP) / few doctors (0.3 per 1000)
B1: explained: little investment means workers have less capital equipment / poor health means more illness and absence

long.q: Extract: Data for 2025. Country Sundra: GDP per head $2,400; 55% of workers in agriculture; saving 9% of GDP; average years of schooling 5; doctors per 1000 people 0.3; population growth 2.8% a year. Country Velmark: GDP per head $48,000; 2% of workers in agriculture; saving 22% of GDP; average years of schooling 13; doctors per 1000 people 3.5; population growth 0.2% a year. Analyse how high population growth could make it difficult for Sundra to raise its living standards.
scheme: B1: with population growing by 2.8% a year, real GDP must grow faster than this for GDP per head to rise
B1: many young dependants mean a high dependency ratio
B1: government spending on schools and health care is spread over more people
B1: families have less income left to save, keeping saving and investment low
B1: more people working the same land leads to smaller farms and low agricultural productivity
B1: if jobs do not grow as fast as the labour force, unemployment and underemployment rise

long.q: Extract: Data for 2025. Country Sundra: GDP per head $2,400; 55% of workers in agriculture; saving 9% of GDP; average years of schooling 5; doctors per 1000 people 0.3; population growth 2.8% a year. Country Velmark: GDP per head $48,000; 2% of workers in agriculture; saving 22% of GDP; average years of schooling 13; doctors per 1000 people 3.5; population growth 0.2% a year. Discuss whether a developing economy like Sundra should try to reduce the share of its workers in agriculture.
scheme: B1: for: agriculture often has low productivity and low incomes
B1: for: moving workers to manufacturing and services can raise output and GDP per head, as in Velmark
B1: for: it reduces dependence on the weather and on volatile world prices for crops
B1: against: agriculture provides food security and may be where the country has low costs and exports
B1: against: farm workers may lack the skills for other jobs, leading to unemployment and overcrowded cities
B1: against: raising farm productivity, e.g. irrigation and machinery, could be better than moving workers
B1: evaluation: success depends on investment in education and infrastructure
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. a gradual shift supported by education, while raising farm productivity, is best

questions.q: What is the opportunity cost of a firm exporting its goods?
o: Selling those goods on the home market
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a number thought the opportunity cost of exporting is importing. It is the next best alternative: selling at home.

questions.q: Country Y has a hot, wet climate and fertile hillside soils. What is the main reason it is likely to specialise in growing coffee?
o: It has the largest population in the world
It places high tariffs on imported coffee
Its climate and soils let it grow coffee at a lower cost than many other countries
questions.why: Countries tend to specialise in products their natural resources and other factors let them produce at low cost.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage to a country of specialising heavily in one export?
o: Its income becomes vulnerable to a fall in world demand or price for that product
It can produce at a lower average cost
questions.why: Relying on one product means a single shock can cut export earnings, incomes and jobs.

questions.q: Which is an advantage to a country of specialising in the products it is best at making?
o: Greater dependence on imports of other products
Structural unemployment if demand for the product changes
More output from the same resources, which can be traded for other goods
questions.why: Specialisation raises efficiency and total output, and trade lets the country obtain goods it does not make.

questions.q: A country's export earnings come 70% from copper, 15% from tourism and 15% from other goods. The world price of copper falls by 20% and nothing else changes. By about how much do its total export earnings fall?
questions.why: Copper earnings are 70% of the total, so a 20% fall cuts total earnings by 0.7 × 20% = 14%.

long.q: Extract: Country Marisol earns 65% of its export revenue from bananas and 20% from tourism. It has a tropical climate, cheap land and many low-skilled workers. In 2025 a plant disease cut banana output, and banana export revenue fell from $3.0 billion to $2.1 billion. Define 'specialisation at a national level'.
scheme: B1: when a country concentrates on producing particular goods or services
B1: which it can produce efficiently / at relatively low cost, and trades for other products

long.q: Extract: Country Marisol earns 65% of its export revenue from bananas and 20% from tourism. It has a tropical climate, cheap land and many low-skilled workers. In 2025 a plant disease cut banana output, and banana export revenue fell from $3.0 billion to $2.1 billion. Calculate the percentage fall in Marisol's banana export revenue in 2025.

scheme: B1: a tropical climate suited to growing bananas

B1: cheap land and plentiful low-skilled labour
B1: explained: low costs of production let it sell bananas at competitive prices on world markets

long.q: Extract: Country Marisol earns 65% of its export revenue from bananas and 20% from tourism. It has a tropical climate, cheap land and many low-skilled workers. scheme: B1: it uses its resources where costs are lowest, so total output is higher
B1: large-scale production gives economies of scale, lowering average costs
B1: export earnings provide foreign currency to buy imports it cannot produce, e.g. machinery and fuel
B1: workers become more skilled and efficient in these industries
B1: more output creates jobs and incomes
B1: higher GDP can raise living standards and tax revenue

long.q: Extract: Country Marisol earns 65% of its export revenue from bananas and 20% from tourism. It has a tropical climate, cheap land and many low-skilled workers. In 2025 a plant disease cut banana output, and banana export revenue fell from $3.0 billion to $2.1 billion. Discuss whether Marisol should continue to specialise in bananas or diversify its economy.
scheme: B1: continue: its climate, land and labour give it low costs and competitive prices
B1: continue: it has established export markets and skilled farmers
B1: continue: moving resources to other products may mean producing them less efficiently
B1: diversify: the disease cut banana revenue by 30%, showing how vulnerable it is to shocks
B1: diversify: changes in world prices or demand make incomes and export earnings unstable

questions.q: A tariff is…
questions.why: Quotas limit quantity; tariffs raise import prices.

questions.q: Why might a government impose a quota on imported steel?
o: To lower steel prices for consumers
To raise tax revenue from imports
To protect domestic steel producers and jobs
To increase the variety of steel available
questions.why: A quota limits the quantity of imports, reducing competition for domestic producers; unlike a tariff it raises no tax revenue, and prices tend to rise.

questions.q: An embargo is…
o: a ban on trade with a particular country or in a particular product
a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
questions.why: An embargo stops trade completely, often for political or safety reasons.

questions.q: A country places a 25% tariff on imported bicycles that cost $240 each. If the whole tariff is passed on, what is the new price of an imported bicycle?
questions.why: Tariff = 25% × 240 = $60, so the price becomes 240 + 60 = $300.

questions.q: Which is a likely disadvantage to a host country of a multinational company setting up there?
o: Profits may be sent back to the company's home country
questions.why: Profits leaving the country reduce the income it keeps from the investment.

questions.q: Globalisation is best described as…
o: a policy of taxing all imports
the growth of the public sector
the process by which economies around the world become more connected through trade, investment and movement of people
questions.why: Lower transport and communication costs and fewer trade barriers have linked economies more closely.

long.q: Explain two benefits of free trade for a country.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. countries specialise where they have a comparative advantage
B1: explained: more output overall, lower costs and prices
B1: a second benefit, e.g. more choice for consumers / bigger markets for firms / competition raising efficiency
B1: explained

long.q: Discuss whether a government should impose tariffs to protect its domestic steel industry.
scheme: B1: a reason for, e.g. protects jobs in the steel industry
B1: a second reason, e.g. protects a strategic industry / stops dumping / raises tax revenue / reduces a current account deficit
B1: a reason against, e.g. higher prices for steel users such as car and building firms
B1: a second reason against, e.g. other countries may retaliate / protected firms have less incentive to become efficient
B1: explained with its effect on consumers, firms or the economy
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. justified only short term, against dumping

long.q: Explain two benefits to a multinational company of locating some of its production in another country.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. lower costs of production, such as cheaper labour or land
B1: explained: lower average costs increase profit or allow lower prices
B1: a second benefit, e.g. avoid tariffs and quotas / be closer to customers / access to raw materials / government incentives
B1: explained, e.g. lower transport costs and better knowledge of local tastes, so more sales

long.q: Extract: In 2025 the car multinational ZenMotor opened a factory in Country Ardesh, employing 6,000 local workers. Ardesh's government gave ZenMotor a ten-year tax holiday. The factory imports most of its components, exports most of its cars and sends its profits to its head office abroad. Define 'globalisation'.
scheme: B1: the increasing integration of the world's economies
B1: through trade in goods and services, flows of investment (e.g. by multinationals) and movement of people and ideas

long.q: Extract: In 2025 the car multinational ZenMotor opened a factory in Country Ardesh, employing 6,000 local workers. Ardesh's government gave ZenMotor a ten-year tax holiday. The factory imports most of its components, exports most of its cars and sends its profits to its head office abroad. Discuss whether Ardesh will benefit from ZenMotor's new factory.
scheme: B1: benefit: 6,000 jobs and incomes, which are then spent in the local economy
B1: benefit: transfer of technology and skills, and new business for local suppliers
B1: benefit: car exports earn foreign currency and help the current account
B1: cost: the ten-year tax holiday means Ardesh receives no tax on the profits
B1: cost: profits sent abroad are an outflow of income, so less of the value created stays in Ardesh
B1: cost: importing most components limits links with local firms and adds to imports
B1: cost: the firm may move elsewhere when the tax holiday ends, causing job losses

questions.q: If a country's currency depreciates, its exports become…
questions.why: Foreign buyers need less of their currency to buy the same goods.

questions.q: The exchange rate changes from £1 = $1.25 to £1 = $1.40. What happens to the dollar price of a UK product that sells for £20?
questions.why: Before: 20 × 1.25 = $25; after: 20 × 1.40 = $28. The pound has appreciated, so UK exports cost more abroad.

questions.q: Which would cause a country's floating exchange rate to appreciate?
o: A cut in the country's interest rates
More imports bought by its residents
Higher foreign demand for the country's exports
Higher inflation than in other countries
questions.why: Foreign buyers need more of the currency to pay for exports, so demand for it rises.

questions.q: In a fixed exchange rate system…
o: the value of the currency is set by market forces alone
the exchange rate changes every minute
the government or central bank keeps the currency at a set value against another currency
questions.why: The central bank buys and sells its currency, or changes interest rates, to hold the agreed value.

questions.q: The exchange rate is $1 = 80 rupees. What is the dollar price of an item costing 2,000 rupees?

long.q: Explain two causes of a depreciation of a country's floating exchange rate.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. a fall in demand for the country's exports
B1: explained: foreigners need less of the currency, so demand for it falls
B1: a second cause, e.g. a cut in interest rates / more imports bought / speculation / higher inflation than abroad
B1: explained, e.g. lower interest rates make saving there less attractive, so hot money flows out and the supply of the currency rises

long.q: Extract: Country Pavano's currency, the pav (P), floats. In January 2025, $1 = P4.00; by December 2025, $1 = P5.00. During the year Pavano's central bank cut interest rates, and Pavano's inflation was 9% compared with 2% in its main trading partners. Pavano imports most of its fuel and food. Define 'floating exchange rate'.
scheme: B1: an exchange rate whose value is determined by market forces
B1: i.e. by the demand for and supply of the currency on the foreign exchange market, without government intervention

long.q: Extract: Country Pavano's currency, the pav (P), floats. In January 2025, $1 = P4.00; by December 2025, $1 = P5.00. During the year Pavano's central bank cut interest rates, and Pavano's inflation was 9% compared with 2% in its main trading partners. Pavano imports most of its fuel and food. A Pavano firm sells a product for P400. Calculate its price in US dollars in January and in December 2025.
scheme: M1: dollar price = P400 ÷ number of pavs per dollar
A1: $100 in January and $80 in December

long.q: Extract: Country Pavano's currency, the pav (P), floats. In January 2025, $1 = P4.00; by December 2025, $1 = P5.00. During the year Pavano's central bank cut interest rates, and Pavano's inflation was 9% compared with 2% in its main trading partners. Pavano imports most of its fuel and food. Analyse how the depreciation of the pav could affect inflation in Pavano.
scheme: B1: imports become more expensive in pavs, e.g. a $1 import rises from P4 to P5
B1: Pavano imports most of its fuel and food, so prices of essentials rise directly
B1: fuel is used in production and transport, so firms' costs rise: cost-push inflation

questions.q: A current account deficit means…

imports of goods and services exceed exports

questions.q: Interest and profits received from investments abroad are recorded in the current account under…
questions.why: Primary income covers wages, interest, profits and dividends earned from abroad.

questions.q: Workers employed overseas send money home to their families. In the home country's current account this is a credit in…
questions.why: Secondary income records transfers such as remittances and foreign aid, for which nothing is given in return.

questions.q: A country's exports of goods are $60 billion, imports of goods $45 billion, exports of services $10 billion and imports of services $20 billion. What is its balance on trade in goods and services combined?
questions.why: Goods: 60 − 45 = +15; services: 10 − 20 = −10; combined = +$5 billion.

questions.q: Which policy is most likely to reduce a current account deficit by cutting spending on imports?
o: Raising income tax to reduce disposable income
questions.why: Lower disposable income reduces spending, including spending on imports.
